Nineteen columns carry the product, the pack, sell price, cost, VAT class, both supply relationships with their own part numbers and costs, price breaks and the image filename — so the client fills it in once and it replaces the placeholder catalogue, DA-20's invented packaging, AC-01's repaired breaks and BE-34's missing cost together. Every rejected row is reported with its spreadsheet row number, the column and what is wrong, and the rest still load. 25 unit tests cover the format, and a round trip through the real screen confirmed it: template downloaded, filled with commas in the product name and category, uploaded, two packs loaded with both supply relationships and their breaks, a category named Gloves, Nitrile created intact, and three deliberately broken rows reported by row number. Item: Build the email flows
Why it matters: OTP verification, order confirmation, restock alerts, supplier notifications to both primary and secondary addresses.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026. A seam like storage.ts, and for the same reason: no provider has been chosen and hosting is IN-01, so everything that could touch a network is confined to mailer.ts. The default driver writes readable .eml files to a gitignored outbox folder, which is right for a laptop and right for a demo — nothing escapes to a real inbox while the catalogue is still seeded test data — and adding Postmark, SES or SMTP means writing one more driver and setting MAIL_DRIVER, with no calling code changed. An smtp driver exists and throws loudly rather than accepting mail and quietly dropping it, which would recreate the exact bug this closes. The wording lives in email-message.ts, which is pure and imports nothing at runtime, so what a customer reads can be tested without a mail server and cannot change with a second driver. Platform conventions are enforced there rather than remembered at each call site: AED in English, VAT shown separately, reference number and never order number, and times written in Asia/Dubai because 23:30 UTC is the following day for the person reading it. Five kinds are wired. Order confirmation on checkout, sent after the transaction commits so a full mailbox cannot lose an order. Restock alerts on the moment a pack comes back in stock — the one automated client-facing message the design allows, fired only on the transition and stamped per subscription so nobody is told twice. Account change decisions to whoever raised them, approved or refused, carrying our reason. Purchase orders to the supplier, to both the primary and secondary addresses because that is what the second address is for, sent separately so one bad address cannot suppress the other. Staff alerts, which are internal and therefore not outreach. The two privacy rules are unit tested on the templates and checked again against what was actually stored: no supplier email names a customer, no customer email names a supplier. A purchase order carries quantities and codes and not a single price. Not built, and deliberately: OTP verification, which is part of a sign-in flow that does not exist yet, and HTML bodies, which are a client design decision. Plain text arrives in every client, cannot break in Outlook, and cannot carry a tracking pixel. Answered by the client 18 Aug 2026: plain text stays. See DEC-30.

Item: Add rate limiting to sign-in
Why it matters: Nothing limits password attempts, so the sign-in endpoint can be brute forced. The spec asks for rate limiting on auth in the hardening phase.
Notes: Matters more with short passwords than with OTP. Built 18 Aug 2026. Five failures against one identifier inside a rolling fifteen minutes and the door closes, answering 429 with a Retry-After header. The window rolls rather than resetting on a boundary, because a fixed window hands out a second allowance the moment the first is spent — twice the intended rate at the moment it matters most. The arithmetic is pure and tested in src/lib/rate-limit.ts (14 tests) so a lockout can be tested without waiting fifteen minutes for one; the database side is src/lib/sign-in-limit.ts. THREE DECISIONS WORTH KEEPING. The limit is keyed on the identifier AS TYPED, not on a user id, because an attempt against an account that does not exist has to be counted too — looking it up first would answer the question the generic ""those details do not match"" refusal exists to avoid, and the lockout message is a function of the wait alone for the same reason. An attempt made while already locked out is itself recorded, so knocking extends the wait instead of running the clock down. And a successful sign-in clears that identifier's failures, so somebody who mistypes twice and then gets in does not carry three strikes into tomorrow — the per-address bucket is deliberately not cleared, since one success says nothing about the four hundred failures beside it. A wider per-address bucket of 30 sits alongside it to catch a spray across many accounts, and it only ever widens the limit rather than lifting it: behind an undecided host (IN-01) a forwarded header is a header anybody can set. New SignInAttempt table, rows deleted once past the window — this is a limiter, not an audit trail, and keeping every mistyped password would be keeping a list of people's near-misses for no reason. Four smoke assertions cover it, run against a fresh throwaway identifier each time so the check can never lock a real person out of the site it is checking.

Why it matters: The admin product screen listed the image files a product references but could not add or replace one, so the only way to give a product a photograph was to put a file on disk and re-seed. That blocked DA-03 and DA-24 from ever being closed by the client rather than by us.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026. Upload, alt text, choose which image the catalogue shows, and remove — on the product screen, through src/lib/admin.ts like every other write, so it is admin-checked, audited and bumps the catalogue version. Files go through the src/lib/storage.ts seam; see DEC-21. Images are accepted on their leading bytes rather than their filename, which turns the DA-25 defect into a refusal at upload time instead of a 400 from the image optimiser at request time. 15 unit tests cover the checks and the key generation. Verified end to end in a browser: a renamed SVG is refused, a real PNG is stored, served and reaches the storefront with no restart, promotion leaves a dense order, removal deletes both the row and the file, and all five actions appear in the audit trail.

Item: The back office had the shop wrapped around it
Why it matters: Every admin and supplier screen rendered inside the storefront header and footer, so warehouse staff worked around a cart and a Browse All Category bar, and the printed order documents carried both onto the paper.
Notes: Fixed 16 Aug 2026. The storefront moved into a (shop) route group that owns the header and footer; /admin and /business-portal now use an operations shell with a left sidebar, per the reference UI the client supplied. No URL changed. Verified in a browser: shop chrome absent from every back-office screen, present on the storefront and the 404, and print media shows no navigation on any of the three documents.

Item: The delivery address printed as raw JSON
Why it matters: The address is stored as a JSON snapshot so editing an address book entry cannot alter where a historical order was sent. Two screens printed that string verbatim, including the delivery note the customer receives.
Notes: Fixed 16 Aug 2026. Parsing moved to src/lib/shipping-address.ts and is shared by the admin order screen, the delivery note and the customer order page, so the three cannot drift. A snapshot that fails to parse now degrades to not recorded rather than throwing.

Item: Withdrawn: the first admin page after signing in was reported as showing the sign-in door
Why it matters: Recorded on 16 Aug 2026 as a defect. It was not one — the finding was an artefact of the test that produced it, and the record is kept so nobody investigates it a second time.
Notes: Withdrawn 16 Aug 2026. The browser test navigated as soon as the sign-in button was clicked, without waiting for the sign-in request to finish, so the session cookie genuinely was not set yet and the door was the correct response. Re-tested twice with one variable changed: waiting for the /api/v1/auth response before navigating gives the signed-in page every time, and not waiting gives the door every time. This also explains why plain HTTP never reproduced it — those requests always carried the cookie. No product change was needed.

Item: The back office looks like the reference operations UI, not like the shop
Why it matters: The client supplied screenshots of the tool they use day to day. Staff processing orders are doing operational work, and the storefront chrome was both a distraction and the reason documents printed badly.
Notes: Agreed 16 Aug 2026. Admin and the supplier portal both use the operations shell; the light sidebar follows the reference rather than the AussieMed navy, chosen so the data on screen is what stands out. The supplier rail lists only the one screen that exists, because an entry leading to an unbuilt page is worse than no entry â€” the rest is BE-21.

Item: The 404 page rendered its header and footer twice
Why it matters: Introduced by the (shop) route group split in c75b2b5 and live for one commit. An unmatched URL was fine; a notFound() thrown inside the storefront — an unlisted product, an order reference that is not yours — came out with two headers and two footers.
Notes: Found 16 Aug 2026 by reading a screenshot, not by a test — every automated check passed. The root not-found carries its own chrome because unmatched URLs resolve above every route group, but when notFound() is thrown inside (shop) that same file renders inside the shop layout, which had already supplied it. Fixed by giving (shop) its own not-found with no chrome, both sharing one NotFoundContent component.

Item: Uploaded files go through a storage seam, not straight to disk
Why it matters: Local disk is right for a laptop and wrong for most hosting: a container filesystem is discarded on every deploy, and two instances behind a load balancer do not share one. Hosting is IN-01 and is not chosen yet.
Notes: Our decision, 16 Aug 2026, taken while building BE-29. Everything touching a filesystem is confined to src/lib/storage.ts behind a driver interface; local disk is the only driver today and STORAGE_DRIVER selects it. Adding S3, R2 or Blob storage means writing one more driver and changing an environment variable, with no calling code touched. What counts as an acceptable image is decided separately in image-file.ts, which is pure and unit tested, so a second driver cannot accept what this one refuses.

Item: Capture supplier sub-order lifecycle timestamps and an immutable status log
Why it matters: Nothing records when a supplier acknowledged, dispatched or delivered a sub-order, so no fulfilment or lead-time question can be answered about any supplier. Unlike most gaps this one cannot be repaired later: a timestamp not captured at the moment it happened is gone, and the same reasoning already applied to SkuBatch under FN-09.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 as part of the capture-early group. One StatusEvent table records every transition of an order, an order line, a purchase order and a pack's stock flag, written from the same service functions that make the change so a transition cannot happen without being recorded. It complements AuditLog rather than replacing it: the audit says an admin changed something and what the row looked like either side, as JSON, for accountability; this records only transitions, in columns, so "how long does this supplier take to acknowledge" is a query rather than a parsing exercise. The actor and their role are on every row, which is what separates the supplier's time from ours — verified by having a supplier acknowledge a purchase order and finding themselves recorded as the actor. It never throws: losing a measurement is a smaller problem than refusing to send a purchase order because a log write failed. Durations are computed by the pure lifecycle.ts, which reports median and P90 rather than an average and says "not enough data" below five samples rather than deriving a percentage from three. The purchase order screen shows how long each stage took and whether the acknowledgement fell inside the supplier's agreed window.

Item: Log every out-of-stock toggle instead of only the current flag
Why it matters: The manual out-of-stock checkbox stores current state only. How long a product has been unavailable, and how quickly a supplier restocks, are unanswerable — and both are conversations the admin has with suppliers.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026. Recorded through the same StatusEvent table as BE-30, as a transition of the pack between InStock and OutOfStock, rather than a table of its own — a stock toggle is a state change like any other, and one query surface is easier to trust than two. Written only on the transition, so re-saving an unchanged SKU does not fill the log with non-events; verified by saving twice and finding one row. How long a pack has been unavailable and how quickly a supplier restocks are now both answerable.

Item: Log storefront searches, especially the ones that return nothing
Why it matters: A search that returns no results is a customer telling you what to stock, and it is currently discarded. For a distributor deciding what to source next, the list of terms that found nothing is one of the most valuable things the site can produce.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026. Recorded on the products page rather than in the search box, because that is the only place that knows how many results the term actually found, and a term that found nothing is the whole point of keeping them. Only submitted searches, never keystrokes. Repeated searches from the same visitor within five minutes count once, so paging through results does not inflate a term and the number that matters — how many searches found nothing — is not dominated by whoever was most persistent. Grouped by a normalised term so forty rows of "gloves" read as one demand, but singular and plural are kept apart deliberately: "glove" and "gloves" finding nothing are two pieces of evidence about wording. The admin screen at /admin/searches defaults to the terms that found nothing, with a link to run each one so the gap can be seen rather than taken on trust.

Item: Record what each supplier has promised: lead time and acknowledgement SLA
Why it matters: On-time means nothing without a promise to measure against. These are numbers agreed personally with each supplier during onboarding, and there is nowhere to put them.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026. The two columns already existed on Supplier; what was missing was any way to fill them in. Both are now on the supplier form, and both accept blank — which means not agreed, and is deliberately not the same as a target of zero, because a target of zero is one every supplier misses. lifecycle.onTimeRate returns null rather than a rate when there is no promise, so a supplier with nothing agreed shows "not agreed" instead of a number that looks like failure. The purchase order screen uses the acknowledgement window to say whether a supplier answered inside it. The register's own warning still stands: these are business inputs somebody has to collect from each supplier before any on-time figure means anything.

Item: Nothing shows which clients are overdue to reorder
Why it matters: In a reorder-first business this is the single most useful signal there is: a clinic that buys gloves every three weeks and has not ordered in five needs a phone call. It is computable from order history alone once there are three orders per client — no new data capture required.
Notes: From spec sections 2.3 C-4 and C-5 and queue Q-3. Unlike BE-30 to BE-32 this is not urgent, because the underlying order history is already being recorded and the calculation can be added at any time. Build it once real clients are ordering; with four test orders it would only ever say insufficient data.

Item: The client account has no Buy Again
Why it matters: A returning buyer has to search for products they have already bought. For a reorder-first marketplace this is the shortest path between the platform and revenue, and it needs no metrics work at all — just their own order history, sorted by how often they buy each line.
Notes: From spec section 4 CL-1 and CL-3. Independent of the whole metrics programme and arguably worth more than any dashboard in it. Depends on nothing that is not already built. Closed 18 Aug 2026 by decision rather than by building it — see DEC-33. The spec asked for this before the client removed the every-item-ever-bought grid on 16 Aug, and building it would have quietly reinstated what they had just taken away.

Item: The dashboard metrics spec is an idea source, not a plan
Why it matters: A specification document generated on 16 Aug 2026 proposes roughly sixty metrics across three dashboards. It was written without sight of this codebase, so it assumes work that is already done and priorities that are not ours.
Notes: Installed at docs/DASHBOARD_METRICS_SPEC.md and framed in CLAUDE.md, with its known errors listed so nobody re-derives them — most importantly that OrderSupplierInvoice is already the supplier sub-order it asks to be created. Its genuinely new ideas were extracted into BE-30 to BE-33, FN-12 and FN-13; the rest is either already registered, already built, or cannot be validated until there is real trading data. Client decision 16 Aug 2026: treat it as idea generation, our judgement ranks above it.

Item: No cost price, so no margin is known
Why it matters: The system records what a product sells for but not what it costs to buy, so nothing can say whether a line, an order or a supplier is profitable. Requested by the client 16 Aug 2026.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026. Rules are pure and tested in margin.ts: a missing cost is unknown and never zero, because zero shows a 100% margin on every product not yet loaded and a figure like that gets believed. Bands treat unknown as its own state rather than a bad one, so nobody is sent to renegotiate a price that is fine. On a product, both suppliers are listed with their own cost and margin — the backup is not decoration, it is what gets bought from when the first cannot supply, and a much worse cost there means the margin shown is the margin on a good day. The headline figure names which supplier it is against, using the same order of preference the purchasing run uses. On an order, cost comes from the purchase order lines the units were actually allocated from rather than the catalogue, because under cross-dock nothing is bought until the cutoff and a cost column on the order line would have had to be a guess. Part-delivered lines report no margin at all rather than one derived from the part that arrived. Admin only, and structurally so: margin-data.ts calls requireAdmin first and nothing under (shop) or business-portal imports it, so cost is not filtered out of a shared query, it is never fetched by one. check:privacy now asserts that no public payload and no supplier-facing page carries a cost or margin field.

Item: AussieMed is the seller of record
Why it matters: Determines who carries the VAT liability and the credit risk, what the customer's invoice looks like, and who chases payment. It had been drifting undecided while the build leaned the other way.
Notes: Decided with the client 16 Aug 2026. AussieMed buys from suppliers and resells: the customer receives one invoice from AussieMed carrying AussieMed's TRN, and suppliers invoice AussieMed separately. Note this reverses the direction the build had taken — orders split into one invoice per supplier, with a database constraint enforcing it, and that split was being shown to the customer. The split is still correct and still needed for picking, delivery notes and paying suppliers; it simply stops being the customer's document. See AC-03 and AC-04 for the consequences.

Item: VAT is a checkout concern only
Why it matters: Settles a question open since the Ex/Inc VAT toggle was removed: whether buyers need to see VAT while browsing.
Notes: Decided with the client 16 Aug 2026. VAT is calculated at checkout and shown on the invoice. It appears nowhere on product pages or listings, which show trade prices only. Consistent with DEC-13. Product tax class still matters, because it decides what checkout charges, but it is never surfaced before then. Closes FE-30.

Item: AussieMed is a cross-dock distributor, not a marketplace
Why it matters: Changes what the platform fundamentally is. Neither side of a transaction may see the other, which rules out the supplier-facing order model the build had grown.
Notes: Decided with the client 16 Aug 2026. AussieMed buys from suppliers and resells; the customer never learns who supplied their goods and the supplier never learns who bought them. Nothing is purchased until a customer has ordered it — the sorting facility is a transit point, never a warehouse, so there is no inventory to hold or reconcile. Goods arrive against a purchase order, are broken down and sorted by customer, then despatched by AussieMed. Depends on DEC-22, which was decided an hour earlier and turns out to be a prerequisite rather than a coincidence.

Item: Two suppliers per item, with automatic fallback
Why it matters: A single supplier per product makes every product only as reliable as one company, and in cross-dock a supplier who cannot supply means a customer waits a full cycle.
Notes: Decided with the client 16 Aug 2026. Each item carries a primary and a backup supplier, each with their own cost, lead time and part number. Purchase order lines default to the primary and revert to the backup automatically when either the supplier is marked unavailable wholesale or that supplier cannot supply that particular item — two distinct flags, because they are different situations. Any line can still be moved by hand before sending. When both suppliers are unavailable the line cannot be sourced and must surface in an exception queue rather than fall silently off the purchase order, because a customer is waiting on each one.

Item: One consolidated purchase order per supplier per day
Why it matters: Sending a purchase order per customer order would flood suppliers and lose the buying power of pooled quantities.
Notes: Decided with the client 16 Aug 2026. Customer orders accumulate through the day; at a configurable cutoff, 5pm Asia/Dubai by default, the system groups every unpurchased line by supplier and sums quantities per item into one purchase order. Anything ordered after the cutoff rolls into the next day. Drafts are prepared for review and sent by hand, with an auto-send toggle in Settings and reachable from the orders section, defaulting to off — nothing commits money to a supplier until a person turns that on deliberately. Purchase order lines lead with the supplier's own part number, with the AussieMed SKU and product name alongside as reference.

Item: Products are hard-tied to one supplier
Why it matters: ProductMaster.supplierId was a required field, so every product belonged to exactly one supplier and could not have a backup. It also meant supplier identity was carried on the product record itself, which is how it reached the browser.
Notes: Completed 16 Aug 2026. ProductSupply replaced it: a SKU joined to a supplier with a rank of Primary or Backup, that supplier's cost, their own part number, their lead time and an availability flag. Built additively first and backfilled, then the column was dropped once nothing read it — the second half of that, on 16 Aug, once OrderSupplierInvoice went with it, since checkout was the last thing using the old field. The admin product form no longer offers a supplier: supply is per pack with two ranks and their own costs, so it belongs beside the SKU and arrives through the BE-04 template. Product lists now show the primary supplier of a product's packs, derived from the supplies rather than stored on the product.

Item: No purchase orders exist
Why it matters: Nothing bought anything. Customer orders were recorded but there was no mechanism to order the goods from a supplier, which is the entire middle of the business.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026. At the cutoff every unpurchased line is pooled by supplier and summed per item into one draft purchase order each, reviewed and sent by hand, with an auto-send toggle defaulting to off. The selection rule is pure and unit tested in src/lib/purchase-plan.ts — 16 tests covering primary preference, fallback when either the supplier or the item is unavailable, pooling across customers, fallback marking, refusing a total when any cost is unrecorded, and determinism so the same demand builds the same document twice. Allocations are written at draft rather than at goods-in, which is what stops a second run ordering everything again; cancelling a draft releases them. Verified end to end: 4 customer orders became 3 purchase orders, 14 units of one item pooled from 3 separate customer lines, a second build created nothing, and npm run check:privacy confirms the document names no customer. Moving a single line between suppliers is deliberately not built — mark the supplier or item unavailable and rebuild, which is what DEC-25 describes and what happens routinely anyway.

Item: Nothing links received goods back to the customers waiting for them
Why it matters: Goods arrive pooled by item, not by customer. Without an allocation record there was no way to know whose units arrived, and no way to answer a recall.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026, completing the cross-dock loop. Goods-in records what physically arrived per line with its batch and expiry, fills the reservations made when the order was raised, stamps the batch onto each allocation and onto the customer's order line, and moves the line to Allocated once it is covered. Short deliveries are treated as the normal case: the rule is pure and unit tested — earliest order filled first and in full, the shortfall landing on the newest, so two clinics get a usable quantity rather than three getting two thirds of a box. Whatever did not arrive stops being reserved and returns to outstanding demand, which puts it on the next purchase order by itself. Over-delivery is refused rather than silently absorbed. Verified end to end on PO-2026-000002 with a deliberate short delivery: 14 units pooled from 3 customers, 13 received, the two earliest filled in full, the third released back to the queue, order left PartiallyReceived, every allocation carrying its lot, and a query on LOT-1001 returning exactly the two orders that received it. That last query is the recall answer the register has wanted since FN-09.

Item: Supplier identity is exposed to customers today
Why it matters: DEC-24 requires that customers never learn who supplied their goods. Three routes currently break that, and one of them ships supplier records to every visitor's browser.
Notes: Closed 16 Aug 2026 in commit 2c966d7 and only marked here on 17 Aug — the row was left Open by mistake while the work itself was finished and guarded. The public /api/v1/suppliers endpoint was removed, supplierId was taken off the Product type and the browser catalogue snapshot, the supplier block came off product API responses, and supplier names came off cart and quote lines. The worst leak was in seeded data rather than code: every product carried a specification attribute labelled Supplier, printed on the product page. npm run check:privacy asserts all of it on every run and has passed continuously since.

Item: Customer identity must never reach a supplier
Why it matters: The mirror of BE-38 and equally load-bearing. A supplier seeing which clinics buy what would hand them the client book.
Notes: Enforced and tested 16 Aug 2026. Purchase orders carry the supplier's part number, our code, the description and a pooled quantity, and nothing else — no customer name, address, order reference or count. npm run check:privacy signs in, fetches a rendered purchase order and asserts that no customer name, email, organisation or order reference appears in the document; it reads only the main region, since the operator's own name legitimately appears in the sidebar. Re-run it whenever a supplier-facing document or the portal changes. The supplier portal itself is BE-39 and still shows customer-derived data.

Item: The supplier portal still shows customer orders
Why it matters: It listed order references and invoice lines drawn from customer orders, which contradicts DEC-24 now that suppliers deal only in purchase orders.
Notes: Rebuilt 16 Aug 2026 on purchase orders. The portal now shows a supplier their own orders, an acknowledge action and a despatch form with optional courier and tracking; it has no route to a customer order at all, which is a stronger guarantee than filtering one. Scoping is structural rather than a check that could be forgotten: no function in src/lib/supplier-portal.ts accepts a supplier id, every query takes it from the session, and a lookup by purchase order number includes the supplier id so another supplier's number does not resolve. Acknowledgement is written once and never moved, because how quickly a supplier responded later feeds their lead-time figures and a stamp that reset on every click would flatter whoever clicks most; despatching implies acknowledgement for a supplier who skips it, without overwriting an existing stamp. Verified in a browser: signed in as supplier1, own orders listed and the other two absent, another supplier's order answered 404, acknowledging set the stamp and removed the button, despatching recorded courier and tracking and left acknowledgedAt unchanged, and no customer identifier appeared anywhere. npm run check:privacy now covers both, so it is a standing test rather than a one-off. BE-21's remaining scope is product and price maintenance by suppliers, which is separate.

Item: Remove OrderSupplierInvoice, the last of the marketplace model
Why it matters: A customer's order was split into one invoice per supplier at checkout. That was right for a marketplace and wrong for what AussieMed is: under DEC-22 AussieMed is the seller of record and issues one invoice, and under DEC-24 the customer never learns a supplier was involved.
Notes: Removed 16 Aug 2026. Checkout writes an order and its lines, and decides nothing about supply — under cross-dock nothing is bought until the cutoff, and the primary or backup is chosen then from whoever can actually supply on the day, so deciding it at checkout was deciding it with the wrong information. The split is not lost, it moved: buying happens on purchase orders and PurchaseAllocation links what arrived back to the customers waiting, which knows the purchase order and the lot rather than only the company. Twenty source files followed: the three order documents are flat, the admin order screen shows where each line's units actually came from once received, the orders list drops a supplier filter that could no longer mean anything, and the supplier screens now show packs they supply and purchase orders raised with them. Six database assertions about invoice splitting were replaced by stricter ones — the money has to add up from the lines themselves, with no intermediate document to hide a rounding difference in — plus a new guard that no order line is allocated more units than were ordered. Verified: 138 unit tests, 22 catalogue checks, 28 database assertions, 26 API contract checks, the privacy check, and all seventeen affected pages driven in a browser with no console or page errors.

Item: No admin queue for enquiries
Why it matters: Capturing quote requests, bulk-buy enquiries and restock demand without anywhere to read them would only have moved the problem.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026 alongside FN-02 to FN-04 at /admin/enquiries. Quote requests and enquiries oldest first, because the oldest unanswered one is costing the most, with anything over two days flagged. The restock waitlist is grouped by pack and ranked by how many people are waiting, which is the number that decides what to reorder. Says plainly on the page that nothing is emailed yet and why.

Item: The account had no way to repeat an order
Why it matters: Reordering was a grid of every item ever bought, one tile each, which duplicated the order history and became unreadable as soon as anyone had ordered more than a few things. "The same as last time" means an order, not a pile of items.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026 at the client's request. The item grid is gone and every past order carries a Reorder button, which opens a review step rather than dropping straight into the basket: a trade buyer repeating last month rarely wants exactly last month, so lines can be unticked and quantities changed first. Priced at today's catalogue prices, not the prices on the original order. Lines that can no longer be bought are shown greyed and marked rather than dropped, because that is precisely the moment a buyer would otherwise not notice something had gone. If the basket already has something in it, the screen asks whether to add to it or start fresh instead of guessing, since both answers are reasonable and getting it wrong silently discards work.

Item: The account showed no account figures
Why it matters: A trade buyer could see a list of orders but nothing about their own account: how much they spend, how often they order, whether they are overdue.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026. Orders placed, total spent, average order and how often they order, from a pure module with 17 unit tests. Cadence is a median rather than a mean, so one holiday shutdown does not rewrite the rhythm, and it stays blank until three orders exist because two orders is one gap, not a pattern. An account noticeably past its own rhythm is told so and offered the reorder, which is the same signal as FN-12 on the admin side, shown to the customer instead.

Item: Orders did not say who placed them or which site they were for
Why it matters: A practice with several sites and several people ordering had one undifferentiated history, so "who ordered this and where did it go" could not be answered.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026. Branches are delivery addresses with a name — a practice with three sites has one account and three places goods go, and orders already pointed at an address, so giving it a name was better than a parallel Branch concept beside it. The account order list filters by branch or shows all of them together. Staff are names on a list the customer keeps, not logins: the question is who ordered this, and answering it does not need passwords, invitations or permissions. Checkout picks a branch and a person, the branch prefills the delivery address, and the staff name is snapshotted onto the order so removing someone later does not blank the orders they placed. Removing a branch archives it for the same reason.

Item: Saved products were an undifferentiated list
Why it matters: A buyer who has saved forty things needs them grouped to find anything.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026. The account groups saved products under the category each belongs to, using the deepest category rather than the department, because "Gloves" is what someone browses by and "Medical Consumables" is not. Only categories with something in them are shown — a list of empty headings is the catalogue tree pretending to be a personal list.

Item: OrganisationStaff.email is no longer collected
Why it matters: The Who orders list records who at a practice placed an order. Nobody on it signs in, so an email address was never used for anything — it was asked for, stored, and read by nothing. Client asked for the field to go on 16 Aug 2026.
Notes: Closed 17 Aug 2026. The column was dropped in migration 20260816160000_drop_staff_email once a migration was being run anyway, as the note said it would be. That migration also had to be renamed to sort after the one that creates OrganisationStaff — Prisma's generated timestamps sort before the hand-named migrations, so the history applied cleanly to this database and would have failed on a fresh one. The shadow-database replay caught it.

Item: Account changes were made silently and with no reason attached
Why it matters: A customer could add or remove a person from Who orders, add a branch, or remove one, and nothing recorded who did it or why. Six months later the account would show a delivery address nobody could account for. Worse, a branch is where medical supplies get sent: an address added by a customer went live immediately, so the next order could ship to somewhere nobody at AussieMed had ever checked.
Notes: Built 16 Aug 2026. One AccountChange model does both jobs — a log of what happened and a queue of what is waiting — because the customer's question is the same either way and two lists would mean checking both. Every change carries a typed reason, which is the one thing about a change that cannot be reconstructed from the data afterwards: the database will always be able to say a branch was removed and will never be able to say the clinic closed. Which changes are held is decided by kind and never by the caller, in account-change-plan.ts, and an unrecognised kind fails closed to needing approval. Staff changes take effect at once because the list is the account's own and holding ''she has left'' would put an order out in the name of someone who no longer works there; branches and the account name are held, because both decide where goods go or what name is on a tax invoice. Customer side: an Account changes tab with the whole timeline and a badge counting only what is waiting. Admin side: a Needs attention screen showing every queue in the back office that has something in it, and the account changes with a field-level diff so approving a phone number does not mean reading seven unchanged address lines. Approval applies the change and records the decision in one transaction. A refusal needs a note, which the customer sees.

Item: A refused form deleted everything the person had typed
Why it matters: React clears an uncontrolled form as soon as its action returns, success or failure alike. Now that every account change needs a reason, being told the reason is too short also silently deleted the name, the address and everything else just typed — so correcting a small mistake cost more than the original entry did.
Notes: Fixed 16 Aug 2026 alongside BE-43. FormState carries the submitted values back, and every field on the account forms reads its defaultValue from them, so a refusal redraws what was typed rather than an empty form. Verified in a browser rather than reasoned about: typing a name and a five-character reason, being refused by the server, and finding both still in the fields.

Item: A purchase order line with no recorded cost was stored as costing zero
Why it matters: buildPurchaseOrders wrote unitCostFils ?? 0, so every line drawn from a supply whose cost had not been loaded was saved as free. Downstream that is indistinguishable from a genuine zero, and the realised margin on the customer order it fulfilled came out at 100% — stated confidently on the screen whose entire purpose is deciding whether a trade is worth doing. The pure planner already modelled the cost as nullable and got it right; the flattening happened only at the database write.
Notes: Fixed 16 Aug 2026 while building BE-34, which is what exposed it. unitCostFilsSnapshot, lineCostFils and PurchaseOrder.totalCostFils are all nullable now, so unknown survives the snapshot instead of becoming a number. A data migration restores the distinction on orders already raised: a zero unit cost was never a real value, because AussieMed does not buy anything for nothing, so every one of them is a flattened null and can be restored without guessing. An order total is set to unknown as soon as one of its lines is, rather than quietly excluding it. realisedCost now separates units received from units costed, and a line delivered in full on a purchase order with no cost is reported as unmeasurable rather than complete. Four purchasing and supplier screens were printing that zero as a real price and now print an em dash. Regression tests cover the null case, the two-purchase-orders case, and that a genuine zero cost still means genuinely free.

Item: Nothing recorded that an email had not been sent
Why it matters: Quote requests, restock requests and enquiries were stored and never sent, and nothing anywhere said so. A silent failure is the only kind that lasts: an empty inbox looks exactly like a quiet week.
Notes: Fixed 16 Aug 2026 as part of BE-05. Every attempt writes an OutboundEmail row before delivery, so a message that never goes out still leaves evidence that it should have. The body is stored in full, because when a customer says they were never told the answer has to be the words that went out rather than a template and a hope that the data behind it has not moved. Failed and queued messages are counted on the Needs attention panel and listed at /admin/emails with the error and a send-again button that goes down exactly the same path as the first attempt.

Item: The whole catalogue shipped with every admin and supplier page
Why it matters: The layout split was meant to stop the storefront's data loading behind the back office, and it did not. The root not-found wraps ShopChrome, which loads every product and hands it to a browser-side provider, and Next includes the root not-found boundary in the payload of every page — so around 150KB of catalogue JSON went out with every /admin and /business-portal response. Visible markup was clean; the data sat in the flight payload where View Source finds it.
Notes: Found 17 Aug 2026 by the new supplier-portal privacy check, which flagged product codes on a screen that renders eleven rows. ShopChrome takes withCatalogue, and the root not-found passes false. Nothing breaks: CatalogProvider already refetches the snapshot on mount, so the only cost is that a search box on a 404 page suggests nothing for the first moment, and nobody is mid-search on a 404. Measured before and after — /admin 160KB to 54KB, /business-portal 154KB to 48KB, /admin/orders to 50KB, and the storefront unchanged. Verified the 404 still renders one header, its footer and its navigation, and that its search suggests normally once the snapshot arrives.

Item: The daily cutoff could not be changed, and no buyer was told what it was
Why it matters: The buying run has always closed at an hour held in a settings row, but nothing could write that row — the value could only be read, so 5pm was effectively hard-coded. Worse, the deadline was invisible on the storefront. A trade buyer deciding whether to order now or in the morning had no way to know which side of the cutoff they were on, and the whole cross-dock model turns on that one time.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. The arithmetic moved into a pure cutoff.ts shared by both sides, so the countdown a buyer sees and the instant the buying run pools against cannot disagree — a customer told they had twenty minutes and then missing the run would be a promise broken by a rounding difference, and there is now a test asserting the two never diverge. Admin gets a picker in Settings showing the exact sentence a buyer will read, before saving rather than after, because this one number is a promise made to every customer. Buyers get a bar under the header on every storefront page, including the 404: the server renders the deadline, which is true whenever the page was built, and the countdown appears after mount and ticks, so there is no hydration mismatch and no stale number. Once the deadline passes the bar corrects its own wording rather than waiting for a refresh that may never come. Two defects the tests caught before shipping: parseCutoffHour returned 0 for an empty field, because Number('') is 0 and 0 is a valid hour — an empty form would have quietly moved every buyer's deadline to midnight; and the invariant test between the two directions found that they name the same instant when standing exactly on the cutoff, which is correct and now documented, with the display erring toward telling a buyer they have missed it rather than the reverse. Note: there is no weekend or holiday rule — the cutoff is daily. If the buying run does not happen at weekends, that is a business rule nobody has stated and it needs its own decision. Answered by the client 18 Aug 2026: the cutoff stays daily. See DEC-28. THE BAR IS SIGNED-IN ONLY from 19 Aug 2026, at the client's request. A visitor who cannot order has nothing to do with a deadline: it hurries them towards a purchase they are not able to make, before anything has told them a trade account has to be approved first. Anyone signed in sees it, buyer or supplier, since it keys on having a session rather than on a role. Two consequences worth having: the exposure recorded on DEC-28 — the countdown promising a weekend run nobody has agreed to work — now reaches only people who already know how the account works, and an anonymous page load costs one settings query fewer, because the cutoff hour is read only when it will be shown.

Item: Reports had nowhere to live in the back office
Why it matters: Customers and Suppliers were each a single list. There was no place to ask the other question a section raises — what did they buy, what did we spend, who is slow — so the answers either did not exist or were buried in a screen built for a different purpose.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. Each section now has its own tabs, Accounts or Suppliers alongside Reports, sharing one definition so the two cannot drift apart. The sidebar keeps one entry per section; the split is behind it.

Item: The first card on Needs attention did nothing when clicked
Why it matters: Account changes are the one queue that lives on the Needs attention page itself, but its card was built from the same list as the others and linked to /admin/approvals — the page the reader was already on. Clicking it changed nothing and moved nothing, so it read as a broken feature. The queue underneath was working the whole time.
Notes: Reported by the client 17 Aug 2026 and reproduced immediately: the card's href was the current path, and clicking left both the URL and the scroll position untouched. It now jumps to the section below and says so on the card, so it no longer looks like a link that goes somewhere else. Confirmed the other cards resolve to real screens rather than being assumed to.

Item: No in-site inbox, and no way to send anything on by email
Why it matters: Needs attention counts what is outstanding right now and returns to zero when the work is done, so anything worth knowing but not doing had nowhere to live — an order arriving, a supplier confirming. There was also no way to put any of it, or an invoice, in front of somebody by email without retyping it.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. A Notification table records the few things worth interrupting somebody about, in words written for a person, deliberately separate from AuditLog and StatusEvent which record everything for accountability and measurement. Orders placed, approval requests and supplier acknowledgements write to it, each keyed on what it is about so a retry or a second click cannot fill the inbox with copies. Writing one never throws: a notification is a courtesy and must not fail the order that caused it. The inbox is at /admin/inbox with an unread badge in the sidebar, read and unread per item, and mark all read. Any item can be sent on as an email to an address typed at the time, with an optional line from the sender placed above the original. The original wording goes out unchanged rather than regenerated, because the person forwarding it has read that text and is vouching for it — regenerating would mean they approved one thing and the recipient received another. An invoice can be emailed from the order screen, next to the document it sends rather than on another screen, to an address prefilled from the order and editable because an invoice usually goes to an accounts inbox rather than to whoever placed it. It is plain text with a link to the printable version: nothing here generates PDFs, and an email claiming to attach an invoice it cannot produce is worse than one that links honestly. When either TRN is missing the email says plainly that it is a record of what was charged rather than a compliant tax invoice, and the form says so before it is sent — AC-03. Everything sent is recorded under Email like every other message, and sending the same invoice to the same address twice does nothing.

Item: A customer could see their orders but never their spending
Why it matters: The account showed a list of orders and a few headline figures on the overview, and nothing else. There was no way to ask what a practice had spent over a quarter, where it went, who was ordering it, or to get the invoices out in a form a bookkeeper could use — all questions a trade buyer asks at budget time and at year end.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request as a Spending tab. Any period: the last three or twelve months, this year, last year, everything, or a custom range. The choice lives in the URL rather than in component state, so a buyer can bookmark last year's figures or send the link to their accountant and both see the same page. Period boundaries are Dubai days and are resolved by one pure module, tested, so the screen and every download agree about exactly which orders fall inside — a figure that disagreed with the spreadsheet under it would make both untrustworthy. Spending is broken down by month, by category, by branch and by the person who placed it, all excluding VAT with VAT shown separately, because a registered business reclaims it and a total that quietly includes it overstates what was actually spent. Invoices are listed for the period with two ways to take them: a printable page per invoice, which any browser saves as a PDF, and a spreadsheet of the lot. There is no PDF generator in this build, so a bulk download of PDFs would need a new dependency and was not invented; what a finance team almost always wants is the figures in a form they can reconcile, and the workbook has one row per invoice with a totals formula, one row per line for pivoting, and a sheet explaining what net and zero-rated mean. Scoping is by session throughout: another account's invoice does not resolve, and no query behind any of it reads a supplier or a cost. The spreadsheet downloads were REMOVED on 18 Aug 2026 at the client's instruction — see DEC-29. The Spending tab, its period handling and the printable invoice are unchanged.

Item: An admin could see every email but could not write one
Why it matters: The Email screen recorded everything the system sent and gave no way to send anything. Any message about an order — it is running late, an item cannot be supplied, the payment is overdue — had to be written from a personal mailbox, which meant it was not recorded anywhere and nobody else could see it had gone.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. Three linked dropdowns on the Email screen: who it is for, which order it is about, and which template to start from. Choosing a supplier switches the recipient list, the template list and the order list to purchase orders in one move, because a template that filled a customer's name into a supplier's message would be a leak the sender did not intend — the customer's details are simply not reachable from that side of the form. Fourteen templates cover what happens to an order: received, running late, part shipped, dispatched, an item that cannot be supplied, ready to collect, payment due and overdue, and the supplier side of chasing an acknowledgement, chasing a delivery, querying a short delivery or a price. Each fills the boxes from the real order and is then edited before sending, so what goes out is what a person approved rather than what a machine generated — the platform's standing rule about automated contact. Templates are pure and tested: every one signs off, none leaves a mail-merge gap when a name is missing, and none of the supplier templates has any customer context to fill in with. Two things are checked on the way out. The address has to be sendable, and a message bound for a supplier must not name a customer, an account or an order reference — checked against the database at send time rather than trusted from the form, matching whole words so a supplier called Dubai Medical is not blocked by a customer in Dubai. A refusal hands the wording back so it takes one edit rather than a retype. Everything sent is recorded alongside every other message.

Item: The printable invoice was a printed web page
Why it matters: An invoice is the document a customer files, forwards to their accountant and pays against. One that arrives with a search box and a navigation menu across the top reads as amateur, and reflects on every figure printed underneath it.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request — their words were that it looked like a direct print of the web page, which it was. The cause was that the project had no print stylesheet at all: fifteen scattered print:hidden utilities and not one @media print rule. So the browser decided everything, and decided badly — screen margins, its own URL-and-date header, backgrounds dropped to save ink, tables sawn through the middle of a row, and a reader whose machine was in dark mode printing white text on navy. There is now a Paper block in globals.css that sets A4 with a 16mm margin, redefines the colour tokens light so the theme cannot follow the page onto paper, opts the status pills back into printing their colour, repeats table headings on a second page and keeps rows and totals off page breaks. The chrome was the harder half: hiding it piece by piece did not hold, because the header, the cutoff bar and the footer live in a layout the invoice never sees and another can be added at any time. A page now marks its document with .print-document and everything that is not that document, its ancestors or its contents is hidden — naming what to keep survives a new layout, naming what to drop does not. The invoice itself was rebuilt in the order a finance clerk reads one: what is this, what do I owe, by when, what for, how do I pay. The amount due is now the largest thing on the page rather than the company name, a balance line appears once part payment has been received, and a cancelled or refunded order says so instead of heading itself Amount due. Verified by screenshotting the page in print emulation in both light and dark.

Item: One colour system for every status
Why it matters: Colour is how a person reads a list of forty orders without reading it. If the same colour means different things on different screens, or the alarming states are not coloured at all, the list stops being scannable and every row has to be read.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request for a universal system across fulfilment, delivery and payment. It found a real defect on the way in: the old StatusPill mapped eleven words and the system uses twenty-seven, so everything unmapped fell through to the same grey — an invoice reading Overdue was rendered identically to a purchase order nobody had sent yet. An overdue invoice looked dormant. The rule is now that a colour says how concerned to be rather than which department a word belongs to: grey resting, blue moving, amber wants a person, green finished, red stopped or late. Learn it on the orders list and it reads the same on an invoice, a purchase order and a supplier screen. Three axes are kept apart because an order genuinely carries three answers — delivered and overdue is the pairing worth acting on and only stands out if both are on screen. Two derived rather than stored: delivery, so it cannot disagree with the order it came from, which also surfaces a dispatch carrying no courier or tracking number as amber where the goods read blue; and payment, which folds in the date, so an invoice that fell due yesterday says so the moment it is opened rather than waiting for a nightly job that would only exist to be forgotten. Every pill carries a shape as well as a colour — roughly one man in twelve cannot separate red from green, and every one of these documents is designed to be printed, often on a mono laser. Rules live in status-tone.ts, pure and tested with 29 tests, one of which walks the schema comments and fails if a status exists that the colour system has never been taught, which is the failure that caused this. Three private re-implementations of the pill were found and deleted, in the account change log, the sent-email list and the past-orders list — the shared component's own docstring had warned against exactly that. The axis is a required prop rather than a guess, because Sent is an email that has gone and a purchase order that has not been acknowledged. A legend on the Settings screen is generated from the same tables the pills read, so it cannot describe a system other than the one running.

Item: Test orders only ever exercised one state
Why it matters: A colour system, a report or an alert cannot be checked against data that only shows one colour. Local data that is uniformly healthy hides every defect in the handling of the unhealthy cases.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. Every one of the seven local orders was Unpaid, and most had no due date at all, so three of the five tones never appeared on a screen and the Overdue defect above could not have been spotted by looking. npm run db:seed:orders now writes ten orders chosen to cover the spread: delivered and settled, delivered and badly overdue, part paid, falling due this week, a split delivery with a line on backorder, a dispatch with no tracking, a pick-up at the counter, one mid-picking with every line at a different stage, one just placed, and one cancelled and refunded. Dates are relative to the run so the spread stays meaningful next month, and SKUs are taken in code order rather than at random so two runs produce the same orders and a before-and-after comparison means something. Every reference is prefixed AM-TEST- and the script clears only those, so orders placed by hand through the site are never swept away. Two things it caught: an order whose lines are all cancelled was totalling AED 0.00, which tells an accounts clerk nothing they can reconcile, and a refunded order was heading its own invoice Amount due.

Item: Categories could be created and renamed, never removed
Why it matters: A taxonomy that only grows is a taxonomy nobody maintains. A category made by mistake stays in the search dropdown and the admin's own screen for the life of the site, and the only way out was a developer with database access.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request — they found they could not remove a category or subcategory anywhere in the admin, which was correct: createCategory and renameCategory existed and nothing deleted. The schema made a naive delete quietly destructive in two ways, neither of which surfaces as an error. ProductCategory cascades, so removing a category takes its product links with it silently; and the parent relation is optional, so removing a department would leave its subcategories pointing at nothing and silently promote them to departments of their own. Both are refused in the service layer rather than in the form, because a server action is a public endpoint and a hidden button guards nothing. The guard that matters is not whether a category holds products — a product usually sits in several and losing one is ordinary tidying — it is whether a product would be left in no category at all, because such a product falls out of every browse path while remaining live and orderable, which is the one outcome an admin cannot see happening and would struggle to find afterwards. Every product currently sits in exactly two categories so that guard cannot fire today; it is there for the real catalogue. A bulk clear of empty categories is offered alongside, because the import creates the supplier's whole taxonomy whether or not we stock it and 125 of the 148 categories held nothing — removing those one at a time is not a feature, it is a chore. It removes empty leaves repeatedly rather than in one pass, so a department whose every subcategory was empty goes in the same run instead of surviving and reading as the button not having worked. Confirmations name what is actually at stake for that particular category rather than asking whether the user is sure, and a delete that will be refused says so immediately instead of asking for confirmation and then refusing. Verified in a real browser end to end on the client's own case: removing the department Hamdani while dubai was still inside it, then dubai, then Hamdani.

Item: Products could not be added one at a time
Why it matters: The bulk upload answers a price list arriving as a spreadsheet. It does not answer the other half of the job — one new line, typed in, usually while somebody is on the phone about it — and there was no way to do that at all.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. Admin > Products now has Add a product beside Bulk upload. The first pack is on the same form rather than a step afterwards, which is the one design decision worth recording: a ProductMaster on its own has no code, no unit and no price, so there is nothing to put in a cart — it is not a product yet, it is a name. Splitting it in two would let somebody stop halfway and leave a row that reads as finished on every admin screen, cannot be bought, and fails db:check's "no product exists without a purchasable SKU" with nothing to tell the person who made it. Products arrive as Draft and going live stays setProductStatus, deliberately a separate decision rather than the last field on a long form. Slugs get a numeric suffix on a clash rather than being refused, because two products may legitimately share a name and nobody should have to invent a difference to satisfy a database. Item codes are checked before anything is written, since that is the refusal a person will actually meet. Verified in a browser end to end, including that a Draft returns 404 on the storefront.

Item: Saving a product from the admin always failed
Why it matters: Every edit to a product — name, description, price class, categories — was refused. The admin could open the screen, change anything, press save, and be told a supplier did not exist.
Notes: Found and fixed 17 Aug 2026 while building BE-55. updateProduct still took a supplierId, looked the supplier up, and wrote the field — but the column was removed from ProductMaster under BE-38 and DEC-25, and the form had correctly stopped sending one. So every save looked up a supplier with a blank id, found nothing, and refused with "That supplier no longer exists." Nothing caught it: typecheck was happy because the field existed on the ProductEdit type and was simply never satisfied, no test covers the seam, and the form's own comment explained at length why there was no supplier field on it — directly above the action that demanded one. It was found by clicking save on an unchanged product, which is the cheapest test there is and had never been run. Worth remembering that a dead field on a type is invisible to every gate this project has.

Item: A refused form threw away everything that had been typed
Why it matters: Being told what is wrong and losing the work in the same instant makes the correction cost more than the original entry. On a long form it is the difference between a usable screen and one people avoid.
Notes: Found and fixed 17 Aug 2026 while building BE-55. React resets an uncontrolled form as soon as its action returns, refusal included, so every AdminForm in the project behaved this way — the new-product form merely made it obvious, because being told "that item code is already used" also deleted the name, the description, the price, the pack and every category tick. Fixed in AdminForm rather than in each action: the submitted FormData is captured and handed back through context, and the fields remount keyed so uncontrolled inputs actually take the restored values, since changing defaultValue on a mounted input does nothing. Doing it per action was rejected — an action that must remember to echo back every field it read is one that will eventually forget one, and the field that goes missing is the long one nobody wants to retype. The FormState type had carried an unused `values` field describing this exact problem since it was written; it is now honoured, and wins over the raw capture so an action can redraw a value it normalised. One trap worth recording: the category ticks silently kept failing after everything else worked, because the hook was being called in the form component's own body, which sits above the provider AdminForm puts around its children. It had to move into a component rendered inside the form. That is the worst shape of bug — the fix looks like it works and one field quietly does not.

Item: Placeholder TRNs so the tax-invoice path can be tested
Why it matters: Without a TRN on either side, every invoice took the unregistered branch and half the tax-invoice code was never exercised. Testing it required inventing numbers, and invented tax numbers are dangerous if they can pass for real.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request for a dummy TRN on the test client. The demo account and AussieMed both carry one now, and both are 9999-prefixed: every real Emirates TRN begins 100, so a placeholder cannot be mistaken for a registration and the test is a prefix rather than a list, meaning one invented later is recognised without anybody remembering to register it. Rules are pure and tested in trn.ts, 16 tests. Every document carrying a placeholder prints TEST DOCUMENT across the top and names which side is a stand-in — this site can email an invoice to a real customer, so a warning in the small print would not have been enough. AC-03 and LG-06 stay open: a placeholder makes the software testable, it does not answer the question. The seller's details are settings rather than code, so the real ones can be entered the day they arrive without a deploy.

Item: Compliance was decided on the customer's TRN alone
Why it matters: A document that calls itself a tax invoice without the seller's TRN is not one. The invoice can be emailed to a customer, so this is a document going out under AussieMed's name claiming a status it does not have.
Notes: Found and fixed 17 Aug 2026 while adding the placeholder TRNs (DA-28). Three separate places asked Boolean(organisation.trn) and nothing anywhere considered AussieMed's own TRN — so putting a TRN on a test customer was by itself enough to head the customer invoice "Tax invoice" and mark the emailable invoice compliant, while the seller had no TRN at all. Under UAE VAT it is the supplier's TRN that makes a tax invoice; the recipient's is required only where the recipient is registered. That rule now lives in one pure function, invoiceCompliance, and reads the seller first. The comment in invoice-email.ts had said "Both TRNs, per AC-03" for as long as it existed, directly above code that checked one — a reminder that a comment describing intent is not a test. The refusal wording also travels with the result now: the email panel used to give a reason of its own, "no TRN is held for this customer", which stopped being true the moment a customer had one and the fault lay at our end instead.

Item: Addresses were free text, with no country at all
Why it matters: Free text means Dubai, dubai, DXB and Dubaie are four places, and that is discovered later by whoever tries to group orders by region. No country field at all means a supplier in Guangzhou and a branch in Muscat cannot be recorded correctly.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request: a country dropdown, the states of each country, and the dialling prefix, on every form that asks for an address. One shared component across the branch form, the supplier form and checkout, because four forms reading these for themselves is how four ideas of an address arise. All 152 countries are listed, with the UAE pinned first — nearly every address here is Emirati and a form whose commonest answer is 230 rows down gets the wrong answer. Subdivisions are held only for the GCC and the countries goods come from, sixteen in all: the full ISO 3166-2 set is several thousand entries and would be shipped into every form that renders a picker, which is the mistake BE-47 was about. A country with no list gets a free-text box labelled with the word that country uses, so it degrades honestly. The label follows the country — Emirate for the UAE, Governorate for Oman, State for India, Province for China — and changing the country clears the subdivision, because Dubai left sitting under Germany looks answered and is not. The dialling prefix is shown beside the phone rather than inside it, and the domestic leading zero is dropped when the two are joined: +971 050... is not a number anyone can ring and is exactly what concatenating the halves gives. Existing free-text values are matched case-insensitively and kept as typed when unrecognised, so nothing already delivering parcels is lost. Rules are pure and tested in geo.ts, 37 tests. Verified by placing a real order to Muscat and reading the stored snapshot and the printed delivery note.

Item: Country stored as a code as well as a name
Why it matters: Grouping or filtering by a display name means UAE, U.A.E. and United Arab Emirates are three places. Printing a code means a delivery note that reads AE.
Notes: Added 17 Aug 2026 alongside FE-39. Address, Organisation and Supplier each carry countryCode as ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 beside the printable name; the code is what anything grouping should read and the name is what gets printed. Both are snapshotted onto the order at checkout, like the rest of the address, so a later edit to the address book cannot move where a historical order went. The delivery note prints the country only when it is not ours — United Arab Emirates on a note going three streets away is noise, and leaving it off one going to Muscat is a parcel in the wrong country. Orders placed before this carry no country and are UAE by definition, since that is all the site accepted at the time. The subdivision column keeps the name emirate: renaming it would touch fifteen files and a migration for nothing a customer could see, and the label above the box is what a person actually reads.

Item: No admin form to add or edit a customer account
Why it matters: Customer organisations can only be created directly in the database. The country and region dropdowns cannot reach a customer record because there is no screen on which to set them.
Notes: Found 17 Aug 2026 while adding country and region pickers to every form that takes an address (FE-39). The client asked for four — branch, customer, supplier, delivery address — and three of them exist. There is no screen anywhere in the admin for creating or editing a customer organisation: no name, payment terms, credit limit, TRN, phone or country. Organisation.countryCode therefore takes its default and can only be changed in the database. The shared CountryFields component is ready to drop into such a form the day it exists. Worth pairing with the customer's own details, since AC-09 payment terms and AC-03 TRN both live on the same record and are equally unreachable today. Built 18 Aug 2026. /admin/customers/new opens an account and /admin/customers/[id] corrects one, sharing a single form for the same reason SupplierForm does — the rules are identical and two copies drift. The country and region pickers from FE-39 now reach a customer, which was the gap that raised this row. Rules are pure and tested in src/lib/organisation.ts (21 tests): a TRN is optional because plenty of buyers are not registered, but a wrong one is refused rather than printed on an invoice they keep, including the 9999 placeholder range; a region is checked against the country's own list rather than accepted as typed; and organisationChanges names what moved without printing a two-thousand-character note into the audit trail. An edit needs a typed reason, the same rule the customer's own forms follow, and a rename also writes an Applied AccountChange so the customer's change log does not become a half-truth about who renamed their account — recorded under the admin's name, not theirs. An edit that changes nothing is refused rather than written as an empty entry. PAYMENT TERMS AND CREDIT LIMIT ARE DELIBERATELY ABSENT: AC-09 has not been decided, and a figure entered before the policy exists is a figure that gets believed; the form says so on screen. The list screen was rewritten from people to accounts, because an account opened here has nobody signing in against it yet and the old query would have hidden the very records this screen exists to manage — customers with no organisation at all are listed separately underneath, so nothing that exists is invisible. Driven in a browser: the placeholder TRN refused with the typed values surviving the refusal, the account created and listed, the edit refused without a reason, the rename saved and logged, an empty edit refused and a duplicate name refused.

Item: Customers could not open an account themselves
Why it matters: Every trade account had to be created directly in the database. A business that found the site had no way in at all, and the only route was an email nobody was watching for.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. A self-service sign-up here is an application rather than an account: AussieMed sells to businesses on credit, so the decision is a person's. Three gates, deliberately different questions — is the form filled in, is the email real, and should we trade with them. A six-digit code proves the address before anybody's time is spent on the application, because a typo in an address becomes the only way to reach a customer about an order they have paid for. The TRN is required at application, per the client: without it no compliant tax invoice can be issued, and asking a month later means reissuing every document sent in between. An application creates a real User and Organisation immediately, both Pending — the alternative, a separate applications table copied across on approval, means every field exists twice and the copy is where the bugs live. Nothing can be done with a Pending account: signIn refuses it by name. Existing accounts default to Approved, since locking out every hand-made account on a migration would be a self-inflicted outage. Rules are pure and tested in registration.ts, 22 tests. Verified end to end in a browser: applied, was refused for a five-digit TRN with the form intact, corrected it, received the code in the outbox, confirmed it, was refused sign-in with "your application is with our team", was approved by an admin, and signed in.

Item: Sign-in tells an applicant why they are being held up
Why it matters: A generic refusal must not reveal which addresses have accounts. But after a correct password, the same generic message to somebody whose application is in a queue is a lie that produces a support call.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 as part of BE-57. The specific reason is given only after the password has been verified — before that, "your application is pending" would tell anyone who typed an address whether it is registered. Unverified, pending, rejected and closed each get their own sentence, and an unverified address gets a link back to the code entry rather than a dead end. Rejections repeat the reason the admin gave, so the applicant can act on it. The OTP path is equally careful: a wrong code and an unknown address get the same answer, resending is silent about whether the address exists, and wrong guesses are counted with a cap of five — six digits is a million combinations, which is plenty against a person and nothing against a script. Renumbered from SEC-04 on 18 Aug 2026: two rows had been added under an id already in use, and npm run register was failing on the duplicate. The original SEC-04 is the older row and keeps the number, because code comments point at it.

Item: Resubmitting an application orphaned an organisation
Why it matters: Every abandoned sign-up left an Organisation row with nobody on it — invisible on every screen, and counted by anything asking how many customers exist.
Notes: Found and fixed 17 Aug 2026 during the browser test of BE-57, by noticing the organisation count was one higher than it should be after cleaning up a test account. An unverified application can be resubmitted, and doing so deleted the user but not the organisation created alongside it. Both go now, in one transaction, and only ever a self-registered organisation with no other users and no orders — one an admin set up, or one somebody else is on, is not the application's to remove. Worth recording because nothing would have surfaced it: no screen lists organisations without users, and the row is harmless right up to the first report that counts customers.

Item: Google sign-in is built and waiting on keys
Why it matters: The button cannot work without OAuth credentials from the client's own Google Cloud project. A button that throws on click reads as a broken site rather than a feature nobody has enabled.
Notes: Updated 17 Aug 2026. The flow is built behind a seam, oauth.ts, in the same shape as storage.ts and mailer.ts. googleEnabled() checks for GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET, and the button appears on the sign-in and sign-up screens only when both are set — so nothing is shown that cannot work. Sign-up via Google skips the email code, since the provider has already proved the address, but still asks for the company details and TRN and is still subject to approval. The state parameter is generated and checked, because without it a third party can hand somebody a finished sign-in link and land them in an account that is not theirs. Still Client-owned: the credentials are tied to the client's account and domain and cannot be produced here. Set both in .env and restart; nothing else is needed.

Item: Invoices were three clicks from the order they belong to
Why it matters: A buyer looking at an order who wants its invoice had to leave for Spending, find the right period, and find the reference in a list — to reach a document about the order already on screen.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. Every order on the Orders tab, open or completed, now carries Invoice and Email it to me. Print is not a separate button: it opens the same page, the browser's print dialogue is what makes the PDF, and a second button calling print() would behave differently depending on whether JavaScript had loaded. Emailing takes no address — it goes to the account's own and nowhere else. A destination box would turn a convenience into a way to post somebody else's invoice anywhere, and the printable page is right there for forwarding. The order is looked up within the buyer's own organisation, so a guessed reference belonging to another clinic finds nothing. The admin's emailInvoice and the customer's emailMyInvoice share one sender rather than two copies of the same document.

Item: Every account screen can be narrowed to one branch
