Why it matters: A practice with three clinics does not have one set of orders, one bill and one shopping list — it has three of each, and the manager asking a question is nearly always asking about one of them.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. Orders already filtered by branch; Overview, My products, Spending and Account changes now do too, through one shared component so the answer to "how do I see just Jumeirah" is learned once. Hidden on an account with a single branch, because a filter with one option is a control that cannot do anything and makes a simple account look complicated. The choice lives in the URL, so the back button works and a branch view can be sent to a colleague, and it is carried across the period picker in both directions — losing the period on every branch click would make comparing two sites over the same months a chore. Two of the four needed a decision rather than a filter. A wishlist belongs to a person, not a site, so My products has no address to filter on: narrowing it keeps the saved products that branch has actually ordered, which is what "my products for Jumeirah" means, and it is a lens rather than a deletion. Account changes are about a branch in two ways — a change to the branch itself, and a change to somebody who orders for it — and both belong under it; changes to the account as a whole appear only under All branches, since showing them everywhere would make three sites look like they each renamed the company.

Item: Category tree completed against Livingstone
Why it matters: A category that does not exist is a shelf nothing can be put on. The client asked for their reference catalogue's taxonomy to be covered in full so every product they intend to sell has somewhere to go.
Notes: Done 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request, by reading livingstone.com.au and diffing against the database rather than adding wholesale. The finding worth recording: the 146 categories already in the tree ARE the Livingstone taxonomy — the read-only extraction mirror they were imported from is a scrape of that catalogue — so the request was already about nine tenths satisfied, and what was actually missing was 21 categories and one whole department, Tattoo & Piercing. Piercing Supplies had been sitting under Beauty, where no buyer would look for it, and moved. Three kinds of thing were deliberately not copied: brand shelves like Heine Products and Welch Allyn Products, which are their merchandising rather than a way of describing goods and which AussieMed's Brand field already covers; First Nation Office Supplies, an Australian procurement classification meaningless to a UAE trade buyer; and New Waxing Range, a promotion with a date on it that Hair Removal already covers. A shelf named after the department it sits in was also skipped. Re-runnable with npm run db:seed:categories, which adds nothing that already exists under the same parent and never removes. The new categories are invisible on the storefront until something is put in them, which is the existing rule for empty categories rather than a fault.

Item: db:check measured categories against the frozen import
Why it matters: A check that goes red when somebody makes a legitimate edit is a check people learn to ignore, and then it stops catching the things it was written for.
Notes: Raised 17 Aug 2026 when the category delete was built, and fixed the same day once adding categories made it fire for real. db:check compared the category count and the department count against catalog.json, which is generated from the read-only extraction mirror — so it measured the database against the taxonomy as imported once, and every edit since read as drift. Removing two junk categories had already made it fail; adding 21 made it fail harder. Categories are database-owned and editable now, so the comparison was answering a question nobody asks. It checks the tree's integrity instead: no category points at a parent that does not exist, no two share a slug, and nothing sits three levels down. Those actually break a storefront, and unlike a count they hold whatever anybody edits. The product, SKU and price comparisons against the catalogue are untouched — those are generated, not edited, so drift there is still a real signal.

Item: A supplier could say whether, but never why
Why it matters: Out of stock and discontinued want completely different things from us — one is a wait, the other needs a replacement — and a single checkbox could not tell them apart, so nobody ever acted on the second.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. Three states now: can supply, out of stock, discontinued, each with a sentence saying what it means for us. When they cannot supply, they may name a replacement from their own range, which appears to the buyer as advice and changes nothing about what is ordered — a supplier silently redirecting our purchase orders is how a clinic receives something it did not ask for. The replacement is cleared when they can supply again, since advice about a moment becomes a suggestion to buy the wrong thing once the moment passes. A thumbnail was added to each row: their part numbers rarely match ours, and the wrong line marked discontinued takes a product off sale for no reason. isAvailable stays a column because the daily buying run and nine other places read it, but it is derived from the new state and written in the same statement, and db:check asserts the two never disagree — that drift is invisible on every screen, so it is asserted rather than hoped for.

Item: The replacement picker offered the whole catalogue
Why it matters: A dropdown listing every pack we sell lets one supplier read our entire range, and infer from it what a competitor supplies.
Notes: Found and fixed 17 Aug 2026 by check:privacy, on the first run after BE-59. My reasoning had been that a supplier suggesting a pack somebody else sends is the useful case, so the picker offered the whole live catalogue. The guard refused it, correctly: BE-39 exists to stop exactly this, and the payload also carried item codes and a rival's company name into the browser. It is limited to the supplier's own supplies now, which keeps the common case — a supplier out of one pack size usually has another — and a replacement from outside their range is a conversation with the buyer rather than a dropdown. The item code was dropped from what is sent too: it was never rendered, and anything reaching the browser that need not is one more thing that can leak. Worth recording that the guard caught a deliberate design decision rather than a slip; the reasoning was plausible and wrong, and only the check knew. Renumbered from SEC-05 on 18 Aug 2026: two rows had been added under an id already in use, and npm run register was failing on the duplicate. The original SEC-05 is the older row and keeps the number, because code comments point at it.

Item: Supplier turnaround was never measured
Why it matters: Acknowledgement time says how quickly somebody reads an email. It says nothing about whether the goods moved, and a supplier can be excellent at one and poor at the other.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request for a tracker between receiving an order and marking it shipped. The timestamps already existed, so this is measurement rather than capture: median and worst-tenth from us sending the purchase order to the supplier despatching it, read from the immutable status log rather than the dispatchedAt column so a row edited by hand cannot quietly improve the figure, and measured against the lead time agreed at onboarding (BE-33). One column matters more than the averages: orders sent, past their promised lead time, and still not despatched. A median of three days looks healthy while two orders sit open for a fortnight, because an order that never ships never enters an average at all. Suppliers with fewer than five completed orders show "only 2" rather than a percentage, following the existing rule that a number derived from three orders is worse than no number.

Item: supplyStatus was defaulted over existing availability
Why it matters: A supplier who had said they could not supply an item had that silently reversed on the new field, while the old one still said otherwise.
Notes: Found and fixed 17 Aug 2026, within minutes, by the db:check assertion added alongside BE-59 — the migration that introduced supplyStatus defaulted every row to Available, including one already flagged unavailable. Backfilled to OutOfStock rather than Discontinued: the old checkbox could not tell the two apart, out of stock is the recoverable reading, and marking a line permanently dead on a guess would take a product off sale for good. The bulk price spreadsheet was writing isAvailable on its own for the same reason and now writes both together. This is the argument for asserting a derived field rather than trusting it: the check found real drift on its first execution.

Item: Customers are emailed as their order moves
Why it matters: A buyer with no idea where their order is rings up. Four well-written emails cost less than four phone calls, provided each one is worth opening.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request for an email at every step. I raised that their own metrics spec says the restock alert should be the only automatic customer email and that four per order is a change of character; they confirmed, so every step it is — with a switch per step in Settings, so turning one off later is a click rather than a deploy and the concern is answerable without me. Three rules keep it from becoming noise. One email per order per step, ever: statuses get corrected, and a customer who gets "on its way" three times stops believing any of them — the OutboundEmail log is the record, so it survives a restart. Nothing is sent when an order is received, because checkout already confirms it and a second email seconds later teaches people ours are not worth opening. And the send never blocks the status change: an admin marking twenty orders dispatched must not have one fail because a mail server is down, so it is quiet and the failure lands in the email log for retry. The wording is worth receiving rather than merely triggered — the despatch email carries the courier and tracking number and, on a split delivery, names what is still to follow. The stage words are the customer's, from order-progress.ts; nobody outside the building knows what Processing means. Verified in a browser: moving an order to Dispatched sent one email, and moving it back and out again sent none.

Item: Status colours are settable by an admin
Why it matters: The five tones carry meaning across every screen. A client who wants them to match their brand should not need a developer, and should not be able to break the meaning while doing it.
Notes: Built 17 Aug 2026 at the client's request. The five tones were given their own CSS variables rather than reusing --success and --danger, which are shared with buttons, form errors and links — recolouring "needs attention" would otherwise repaint every amber button on the site, which is not what anybody means by changing a status colour. A chosen colour is emitted as one declaration on the document root, so one change reaches every pill, rail, dot and progress bar at once. Unset tones emit nothing at all, so an untouched site keeps its own tokens including their dark variants. The pale background behind each pill is derived with color-mix from the ink rather than picked separately: nobody wants to choose ten colours, and a hand-picked pair is how you get an unreadable one. Hex is validated on write and again where the style block is built — a stored value is not a safe one to interpolate into a stylesheet just because we stored it. What is deliberately NOT settable is which status gets which tone: that mapping is the meaning, and making it editable would let an overdue invoice be turned green, which is not a preference but a way to hide a problem.

Item: The order seed crashed once a test order had shipped
Why it matters: A re-seed that works only until the data gets interesting is not much of a re-seed, and the failure was a wall of Prisma internals rather than a reason.
Notes: Found and fixed 17 Aug 2026 while resetting test data after the BE-61 browser test. PurchaseAllocation.orderItemId is RESTRICT rather than cascade, and rightly so — an allocation records which supplier batch filled which customer line, and that is how a recall is traced to the clinics that received it, so losing it with an order would be losing the only copy. Once a test order had been through a despatch it had allocations, and deleting it was refused. The seed now clears allocations for its own orders first, which is safe because everything in its scope is prefixed AM-TEST-. Worth recording because the constraint is correct and the seed was wrong: the fix is not to weaken the constraint.

Item: The whole category tree is visible, stocked or not
Why it matters: The site should advertise the range AussieMed sells, not the 23 categories the 71 placeholder products happen to fill. Hiding the rest made a supplier of medical, dental, laboratory, cleaning, kitchen, office, pet and tattoo supplies look like a supplier of eight departments, and gave the client no way to see on the storefront the tree they had just approved.
Notes: Decided with the client 18 Aug 2026, reversing DEC-16 and reopening FN-11. All 12 departments now appear on the front page and all 154 sub-categories in the Browse All menu. The products page carries the whole tree while a buyer is browsing, and still hides zero-count categories once a search term or a brand filter is in play, because there a category list is a filter and a filter offering a choice that returns nothing is noise. An unstocked category no longer shows a bare no-results grid: it says the category is part of the range, the products are not on the site yet, and offers an enquiry that carries the category name through to the admin queue. The wording and the decision behind it are pure and tested in src/lib/empty-state.ts, so the same judgement cannot be made two ways in two places. Nothing was added to the database — the tree from DA-30 was already there; this row is only about what the storefront shows. Tattoo & Piercing has no category photograph, so its tile falls back to the navy block until one is supplied (DA-03).

Item: Every sub-category filled with sample products
Why it matters: The client asked on 18 Aug 2026 for at least five products in every sub-category, so the whole tree can be browsed and tested before the real catalogue lands. There is no real range to fill it with yet (DA-01), so the filler is invented.
Notes: Built 18 Aug 2026. 727 products across 149 sub-categories, topping each up to five and leaving the five that already held more alone. They are deliberately obvious: named ""Pet Toys sample product 1"", item code SAMPLE-PET-TOYS-1, and carrying the placeholder notice every seeded product already shows on its page. Prices are AED 5.00 to AED 249.50 on a clean half-dirham, derived from a hash of the category slug so a re-seed never reprices the catalogue and yesterday's screenshot still matches today's site. One in five is out of stock so the in-stock filter and the Notify Me form have something to act on. Rules are pure and tested in src/lib/sample-products.ts; the seeder is prisma/seed-samples.ts, safe to re-run and reversible with npm run db:seed:samples -- --remove, which refuses to delete a sample an order references rather than breaking that order's history. ONE RULE IDENTIFIES THEM, because three things depend on it: the catalogue seed must not retire them (they are never in catalog.json, so its sweep would switch all 727 off), db:check must not count them as drift (the trap DA-27 dug this project out of, and it now reports them instead), and --remove has to find them again. Bug found on the first run and worth remembering: the storefront caches the catalogue against a version stamp in Settings, so a script that writes products without bumping it leaves a running server serving the catalogue it read at boot — 727 products were created and the site kept showing 60.

Item: Remove the sample products before launch
Why it matters: 727 invented products are on the storefront. They are labelled as samples on every page, but a live site that lists them is a site advertising stock that does not exist, and a buyer can put one in a basket today.
Notes: Raised 18 Aug 2026 alongside DA-33, and deliberately a P1 launch blocker rather than a note on it — the same shape as SEC-01 test credentials and IN-06 noindex. It is one command: npm run db:seed:samples -- --remove. Do it when the real catalogue is uploaded (DA-01), not before, since removing them empties 149 categories again. The removal reports any sample an order references instead of deleting it, so run it and read the output rather than assuming it is clean.

Item: The duplicate Oral Care shelf was merged
Why it matters: Beauty, Skin & Personal Care carried two categories both called Oral Care. It came in with the import and was invisible while one of them was empty; making the whole tree visible (DEC-27) and then filling it (DA-33) put the same shelf name twice in one department with different contents behind each.
Notes: Merged 18 Aug 2026 on the client's decision. Fixed in the catalogue build rather than only in the database, or the next re-seed would have brought it back: buildCategoryTree now folds a category into a sibling of the same name under the same parent, and maps any product filed under the later copy onto the first, so a merge can never cost a product its category. Deliberately only among siblings — the same name under two DIFFERENT departments is not a duplicate, and merging Bags under Kitchen with Bags under Cleaning would file bin liners with sandwich bags. The nine remaining repeated names are all of that kind and were left alone. In the database the twin held five sample products and no real ones, so those went with it and the shelf that kept the three real products stayed.

Item: npm run db:seed had been broken since 16 August
Why it matters: The seed threw on its first product because it still wrote ProductMaster.supplierId, a column BE-40 removed. Nobody noticed for two days because nobody re-seeded — and when somebody finally did, it had already deleted every product-category link before it crashed, leaving all 60 real products uncategorised.
Notes: Found and fixed 18 Aug 2026 while merging the duplicate category. Three separate faults in one command, all of the same shape: a seed built when the catalogue owned everything, still asserting ownership over things that have since moved out of it. (1) It wrote a supplier onto the product. Supply is ProductSupply now, a primary and a backup with a cost each (DEC-25), and the catalogue file has no business asserting who supplies a line. (2) It cleared every product-category link, every price tier, every attribute and every image before rebuilding them from the file — which would have stranded all 727 sample products, emptied the 149 categories they fill and failed db:check's own uncategorised assertion, from a command whose whole job is to be safe to re-run. Those sweeps now skip samples. (3) It suspended every supplier not named in the file, and did suspend two working ones on this database, one with a portal login, eleven supply terms and two purchase orders. That sweep is gone: suspending a supplier is a decision somebody takes on /admin/suppliers, not something a frozen scrape decides. The lesson is the one DA-27 recorded and this repeats: as data moves out of the imported catalogue and into the hands of people who edit it, everything that still treats the file as the authority becomes a way of quietly undoing their work.

Item: The seed re-created categories that had been deleted
Why it matters: Every category an admin removed came back on the next re-seed, because the seed upserted the whole tree from catalog.json on every run. It re-created Piercing Supplies under Beauty on 18 Aug — a shelf that had been moved to Tattoo & Piercing, where a buyer would actually look for it, with the empty original removed on purpose.
Notes: Fixed 18 Aug 2026. The seed now creates the tree ONCE, on an empty database, and never touches it again: the database owns the taxonomy. That is the same conclusion DA-27 reached when db:check stopped comparing categories against this file — a frozen scrape cannot be the authority on a taxonomy people edit, and there is no way for the seed to tell a category deleted deliberately from one that never existed. A category in the file that is not in the database is now REPORTED on every run rather than silently recreated, because a product filed only under a removed shelf is something to look at rather than something to fix by resurrecting the shelf.

Item: The cutoff runs every day, weekends included
Why it matters: The daily purchase-order cutoff had no weekend rule because none had been agreed, and the buyer-facing countdown sits on every storefront page. On a Saturday it counts down to a run nobody has agreed to work.
Notes: Decided by the client 18 Aug 2026, asked with the alternatives of a Monday-to-Friday week, a Sunday-to-Thursday week, and weekdays plus UAE public holidays. Their answer: leave it daily. WHAT THAT COMMITS THE BUSINESS TO, recorded so it is a choice rather than an oversight: the countdown tells a clinic on Saturday afternoon that ordering within the next few hours puts them in today's run, so somebody has to review and send the weekend drafts for that to be true. Auto-send is off by default, so nothing goes to a supplier unattended — the exposure is a promise made on the storefront, not an order placed by accident. Revisit if weekend orders start sitting until Monday: the arithmetic is already in one place (src/lib/cutoff.ts, pure, 24 tests, shared by the buying run and the buyer's countdown so the two cannot diverge), and a weekday rule would be a change to that file and nothing else.

Item: Customers get printable invoices, not spreadsheets
Why it matters: Asked on 18 Aug 2026 how bulk invoice downloads should work, given that a folder of PDFs would need two new dependencies. The client's answer was to remove the spreadsheets instead.
Notes: Done the same day. The customer's bulk .xlsx of invoices and the per-invoice spreadsheet link are gone, along with src/lib/invoice-workbook.ts, the download actions and the button component. invoicesForPeriod went with them: the bulk download was its only caller, and a query nobody calls is a query nobody maintains. WHAT CUSTOMERS STILL HAVE: the Spending tab itself, with the period in the URL so it can be bookmarked and shared, the breakdown by month, category, branch and person, and a printable page per invoice their browser saves as a PDF. WHAT THIS COSTS: an accountant reconciling a quarter now retypes figures rather than pivoting them, and there is still no way to take many invoices at once. That is the trade the client chose, and DF-05 already carries the wider question of downloadable documents. The exceljs dependency STAYS — the admin catalogue upload template (BE-04), the supplier's supply-terms workbook (BE-21) and the generated register spreadsheet all use it, and all three are inputs the business actually works from rather than exports nobody asked for.

Item: Email stays plain text
Why it matters: Every message the platform sends is plain text. It was built that way because the alternative meant inventing a brand email look nobody had approved, and the question was left open rather than decided by default.
Notes: Decided by the client 18 Aug 2026, asked with the alternatives of a branded HTML layout and HTML for customer-facing mail only. Their answer: leave it plain. The reasons that make this a decision rather than a shortcut: plain text renders on every client, on a phone and through a hospital mail filter; it cannot carry a tracking pixel, which matters when the recipients are clinics; and it reads as though a person wrote it, which suits a trade supplier. What it gives up is a logo and any layout beyond line breaks, so an order confirmation is a list rather than a table. All the wording lives in src/lib/email-message.ts, which imports nothing at runtime and is tested on its own, so adding an HTML body later is a change in one file rather than a rewrite — the seam is already there if a designer ever supplies a template.

Item: Stock is in or out, and quantities are never tracked
Why it matters: Products carry a single in-stock flag with no quantities anywhere, so there are no low-stock warnings and no backorders. Left open since the build began as a question about whether real stock levels were needed.
Notes: Decided by the client 18 Aug 2026, in their words: quantity is not tracked because it is not important to us. It is also the answer the model already implied — this is pure cross-dock (DEC-24, DEC-25), nothing is bought until it is sold and the facility is transit only, so there is no stock of AussieMed's to count. Any number would be the supplier's, kept accurate by hand without a feed from them, and a stale figure saying 200 when there are 6 is worse than no figure because a buyer believes it. What the flag actually means is whether a supplier can supply, which ProductSupply.isAvailable already carries per supplier with automatic fallback to the backup. WHAT THIS LEAVES: a buyer ordering 40 boxes cannot see whether that is routine, and finds out through goods-in, where the short-delivery rule fills the earliest order in full and lands the shortfall on the newest rather than giving three clinics two thirds of a box each. That is the designed behaviour, and it is the honest one without a live supplier feed.

Item: Postgres on managed hosting for production
Why it matters: The site runs on a SQLite file, which is right for building and wrong for a live storefront: one writer at a time, and nowhere to keep a file on hosting that replaces the disk on every restart.
Notes: Decided by the client 18 Aug 2026, asked with the alternatives of staying on SQLite behind a VPS with a real disk, or deferring until hosting is chosen. Their answer: Postgres, managed. The build has been kept portable for exactly this — every money column is an integer of fils, no SQLite-only SQL anywhere, and the reports aggregate in memory rather than in dialect-specific queries — so the switch is a connection string, a regenerated migration history and re-running the gates. It does not unblock anything today and it is not done until it is running: IN-02 stays open, and IN-01 hosting is the client's to choose. The trap this decision immediately exposed, and closed, is recorded on IN-02: case-insensitive search does not survive the move by itself.

Item: Reordering is from a past order, not from a list of everything ever bought
Why it matters: The spec asked for a Buy Again list — every product the account has ordered, each with an add-to-cart. The client had already removed exactly that grid from the account area on 16 Aug 2026 in favour of reordering a specific past order.
Notes: Confirmed by the client 18 Aug 2026, asked with the alternatives of building it as specced or adding a bought-before filter to the products page. Their answer: close it, reorder from an order is the way. Recorded as a decision so the row does not sit open looking like something nobody got round to, and so nobody rebuilds it from the spec in six months. WHAT COVERS THE NEED TODAY: Reorder on any past order, opening a review screen where lines can be unticked and quantities changed, priced at today's prices and asking whether to merge with or replace the current basket; My products, which is what the buyer chose to save, with a quantity stepper and an add to cart on each card; and the Orders tab, split into open and completed. WHAT IS STILL TRUE: a buyer who wants the gloves they bought three months ago has to find the order they were on. If that turns out to hurt once real clients are ordering, the smallest honest answer is a bought-before filter on the products page rather than a second grid.

Item: The client's clinical category list was added
Why it matters: The client supplied a surgical and ward-supply taxonomy — eighteen names covering theatre textiles, procedure packs, vascular access and nursing supplies — and asked for anything missing to be added as a department or a sub-category.
Notes: Added 18 Aug 2026 by diffing against the tree rather than adding wholesale, the same method as DA-30. Two departments and twelve categories: Surgical & Theatre (Apparel, Drapes, Gowns, Operating Theatre Consumables, Sterile Procedure Packs, Surgical Instruments & Sterilization) and Nursing & Patient Care (Nursing Supplies, Personal Care, Vascular Access, Fluid Management), plus Gloves under Protective Wear PPE and Exam & Diagnostic Supplies under Instruments & Diagnostics. Two new departments rather than eleven more shelves in Medical Consumables, which already held twenty-one and covered no surgery at all. SEVEN OF THE EIGHTEEN WERE NOT ADDED, because the tree already carries them under wording it chose earlier and a second shelf meaning the same thing is the defect merged out of Beauty the same morning (DA-35): Incontinence is Incontinence Care; Respiratory is Respiratory Management; Skin Care and Wound Care already exist; Personal Protection is the Protective Wear PPE department itself; OR & Surgery Supplies is the same goods as Operating Theatre Consumables, which is the term a UAE buyer uses. Namic Fluid Management was added as Fluid Management — Namic is a BD product brand, and a shelf named after one brand stops making sense the day the brand changes, which is why Heine Products was not copied either. Gloves was added ALONGSIDE Hand Protection rather than replacing it: the umbrella also covers barrier creams and sleeves, but Gloves is the word buyers search and the biggest line in the catalogue. Filled to five products each by the sample seeder (DA-33), so nothing new is an empty shelf. NOTE: neither new department has a category photograph, so both tiles fall back to the navy block until DA-03 lands. seed-category-gaps.ts was replaced by prisma/seed-categories.ts, which holds both sources labelled and dated behind one implementation — two scripts doing this would have been two copies of the same upsert logic, and the second one written is always the one that stops matching the first.

Item: Henry Schein's taxonomy added, dental made comprehensive
Why it matters: The client asked for every category on henryschein.com.au, with the dental listings made comprehensive. Their tree is dental-first and three levels deep; ours is two, asserted by db:check and assumed by the breadcrumb, the Browse menu and the filter sidebar.
Notes: Added 19 Aug 2026, read from the site rather than invented. The client's decision was to promote their top level to departments so their second level lands as our sub-categories and the detail survives: 24 departments and 263 sub-categories, taking the tree to 445 categories and 37 departments. Their third level is not carried — Hand Files is one shelf rather than seven, which is where a buyer stops narrowing anyway. FIVE RENAMED, because their names are only unambiguous inside a dental-only catalogue: Laboratory to Dental Laboratory (we already have one full of glassware and chemicals), Instruments to Dental Instruments, Equipment to Dental Equipment, X-Ray to Dental X-Ray, and Burs split into Dental Burs and Laboratory Burs because their third level is the useful part and the two groups repeat names. NOT COPIED: Clearance, New Products and Price Drop are merchandising; Zany Jackets, Carriere Motion, Mini-Molds, Nitanium Molar Rotator, Nitanium Palatal Expander, TransForce and Twin Force Bite Corrector are brands, and a shelf named after one stops making sense the day the supplier changes. THE OLD DENTAL DEPARTMENT WAS ABSORBED, not left beside them: its twenty shelves duplicated the new departments by name, which is the fault merged out of Beauty the day before (DA-35). Its one real product, a Myerson Dura-Post, was rehomed to Restorative & Cosmetic / Pins & Posts first; 99 samples went with the shelves; the migration refused to delete anything it could not account for. All 263 new shelves filled to five by the sample seeder at the client's request, so the catalogue is now 2,057 products of which 1,997 are invented — DA-34 matters more than ever.

Item: SQLite's query-parameter limit broke every storefront page
Why it matters: At 2,057 active products the catalogue load exceeded the number of parameters SQLite accepts in one query, and every page of the storefront answered 500 with Prisma P2029. It appeared the moment the dental tree was filled and nothing smaller would have shown it.
Notes: Found and fixed 19 Aug 2026, minutes after DA-39 filled the tree. Prisma resolves each included relation with an IN clause carrying one parameter per product, and eight relations across two thousand products is past what SQLite will take. The catalogue now loads in cursor batches of 200, so each round stays bounded however large the catalogue grows — ordered by id for the cursor and sorted by name afterwards, because a cursor needs a unique column and a product name is not one. WORTH RECORDING FOR WHAT IT SAYS ABOUT THE SHAPE OF THIS PROJECT: the failure was total, instant and invisible to every gate. 601 unit tests, typecheck, the register check and db:check were all green while the storefront served nothing but 500s, because none of them loads a page. It was found by fetching the home page. The register has said since the beginning that this design suits 71 products and not thousands; this is the number where that stopped being a note and became an outage. Postgres will raise the ceiling (DEC-32) and BE-10 removes the need to hold the catalogue at all.

Item: The whole dental tree sits under one Dental department
Why it matters: Promoting Henry Schein's top level to departments (DA-39) put twenty-four dental tiles on the front page beside Kitchen and Pet Care. The client asked for them grouped under one Dental category, detailed list and all.
Notes: Done 19 Aug 2026, and the shape was chosen on measurement rather than preference. Flattening all 287 dental shelves into one department was costed first and rejected: twelve names collide as siblings — Accessories belongs to Dental Burs, Crown & Bridge, Impression, Dental Instruments and Restorative & Cosmetic at once, Polishers to two kinds of bur — so 27 shelves would have merged into meaningless single shelves or needed qualifying in brackets. THE TREE CARRIES A THIRD LEVEL FOR DENTAL INSTEAD: Dental > Endodontics > Hand Files, one tile on the front page, 14 departments again, every shelf keeping its own name. What that touched: Category gained an optional children, so the other thirteen departments stay two deep and no screen has to pretend otherwise; catalog.ts builds to whatever depth the tree has and rolls every count up through it, or Dental would have read as empty while holding 1,315 products; a product's category path is now ordered by DEPTH rather than by a comparator that only knew how to put a department first, which was enough at two levels and silently wrong at three; the filter sidebar opens the third level only for the shelf the buyer is inside, because 263 dental sub-shelves at once is a wall rather than a filter; the categories API carries the tree to whatever depth it has and counts through all of it; the sample seeder fills LEAVES only and files each product against every ancestor, so a middle level does not get five products of its own on top of the nineteen shelves beneath it. db:check now asserts no more than three levels, and still refuses a fourth, because nothing renders one. The seeder expresses the nested shape, so a fresh database reproduces it — and Livingstone's twenty old dental shelves were removed from that file, because leaving them would have had it restore the absorbed department on the next run, which is DA-37's fault arriving by a different door.

Item: Categories were left answering to an awkward URL
Why it matters: A slug is disambiguated with a numeric suffix when its plain form is taken, which was true when the dental disciplines were created and stopped being true when the old Dental shelves were absorbed an hour later. Endodontics answered to /products?category=endodontics-2 while the obvious address showed the not-stocked-yet page.
Notes: Tidied 19 Aug 2026 by scripts/tidy-category-slugs.ts, which hands a freed plain slug back to the SHALLOWEST claimant — three shelves are called Endodontics, and the one a buyer means when they type it is the discipline, not Dental Burs > Endodontics. Eleven slugs recovered. Found by driving the site rather than by any check: /products?category=endodontics answered 200 with an empty page, which is the worst kind of wrong because nothing reports it. Sample product slugs still embed the suffix they were generated against, so a few read sample-endodontics-2-3 under a category now called endodontics; they are invented products due for deletion at launch (DA-34) and renaming 2,000 rows to tidy a string nobody reads is not worth the churn.

Item: The filter bar is a box of its own, opened where the buyer clicked
Why it matters: The filter was an unframed column that scrolled with the page. At 445 categories, arriving from a front-page tile landed a buyer at the top of an alphabetical list with the category they had just chosen somewhere below the fold, and scrolling to find it scrolled the products away as well.
Notes: Built 19 Aug 2026 at the client's request. Three things, and the third is the one that matters. It is BOXED: a bordered panel with its own header carrying a Clear all that resets category, brand and availability together, replacing the clear-category link buried in the list. It SCROLLS ON ITS OWN: sticky beside the results, capped at the height of the screen, so a fifty-row department can be read without the products leaving with it. And it OPENS ON WHAT WAS CHOSEN: the active entry is marked at all three levels and src/components/FilterScroll.tsx scrolls the box — not the page — to it on mount, a third of the way down so the shelves beneath an open category are visible too, and not at all when it is already in view. Deliberately scrollTop rather than scrollIntoView, which scrolls every ancestor that can scroll and drags a sticky sidebar's whole page down with it. CONSISTENCY IS STRUCTURAL rather than a convention: the frame moved out of the products page and into the component, so the one route it appears on — every category, every search, every brand view — cannot dress it differently on one of them. Verified by arriving the way a buyer does, clicking Dental on the front page and finding it in view, and by a deep link to a third-level shelf, which opens the box scrolled to Hand Files with the page still at the top.

Item: Filter sections fold, and price and volume breaks were added
Why it matters: The brand list is every brand in whatever the buyer is looking at — twenty-six on the full catalogue — sitting open between them and the bottom of the panel. And the only things that could be filtered were category, brand and in-stock, on a trade site whose whole argument is volume pricing.
Notes: Built 19 Aug 2026 at the client's request. Every section folds; Brand starts SHUT and opens by itself when a brand is in force, because a filter you cannot see is a filter you cannot clear. Two filters added: a PRICE WINDOW, two boxes and an Apply rather than a slider — trade buyers arrive with a figure in mind and a slider makes them hunt for a number they already know, besides being hard to work with on a phone or a keyboard — and VOLUME PRICE BREAKS, which answers what is worth ordering by the box and is the reason a buyer is on this site rather than a pharmacy's. Both live in the URL with everything else, so a filtered view can be sent to whoever approves the order. The rules are pure and tested in query.ts: a window is inclusive at both ends, a window typed backwards (100 in From, 10 in To) is read the way it was meant rather than returning nothing, and a break counts on ANY pack because the carton is usually where the discount is. URL building moved to src/lib/filter-href.ts with six tests of its own, because a server component may not hand a function to a client one — the price boxes needed to build their own links and a second copy of that rule is how two of them drift. TWO DEFECTS FOUND WHILE DRIVING IT: applying a filter used to carry the show-more window into a different result set, so changing a category showed ninety-six products of something else; and choosing a brand made the Brand section vanish, because filtering to one brand leaves one brand in the list and the section was drawn only when there was more than one. A price of abc or -5 in the query string is dropped rather than passed on as NaN, which compares false against everything and empties the page. THE IN-STOCK FILTER WAS THEN REMOVED, at the client's request the same day, and it is the right call for a reason worth writing down: this business holds no stock. Nothing is bought until it is sold (DEC-24), so the flag means a supplier can supply the line (DEC-31) — and a buyer ticking "in stock only" reasonably reads it as a promise about a shelf somewhere. Offering a control that answers a different question to the one it appears to ask is worse than not offering it. The volume-breaks toggle that sat beside it moved under Price, where it belonged anyway. The parameter itself is untouched: inStock=1 in a URL still filters and the v1 API still takes it, since the API's callers are not making that misreading.

Item: The header is one bar, and it gets out of the way
Why it matters: The header was two stacked rows — a white utility bar above a navy nav bar — taking about 140 pixels off every screen before a buyer saw a product, and staying there for the whole scroll.
Notes: Rebuilt 19 Aug 2026 to a reference the client supplied: one white rail floating on the navy ground, logo, navigation, search and account across it. 80 pixels rather than 140. NOTHING WAS LOST IN THE MERGE — the department menu became the Shop dropdown, the search moved behind its own button and opens the same typeahead over the same 2,057 products, and the cart, quote list and account button are where they were. The Home link went, because the logo has always done that job. Request access was added beside Sign in for signed-out visitors only: a trade account has to be applied for and approved, so somebody arriving for the first time needs that door before the one marked sign in, and has nothing to sign in with. THE BAR HIDES GOING DOWN AND RETURNS ON THE FIRST FLICK UP, without having to reach the top of the page — on a catalogue this size a buyer scrolls a long way, a permanently sticky bar is permanently in the way, and one that only comes back at the top makes people scroll miles to reach the search. Two details that are the whole difference between working and irritating: a four-pixel deadband, because the sub-pixel jitter a trackpad makes at the end of a flick otherwise reads as a change of direction and the bar flaps; and it never hides while the Shop menu, the search or the phone menu is open, since a menu that scrolls away while it is being read looks like a fault. Escape now closes the search panel too — it used to close only the suggestion list, which left the panel open and the bar pinned. THE SEARCH BOX CAME BACK INTO THE BAR the same day, at the client's request: behind a button it was a click away from the thing buyers use most on a catalogue of 2,057 products, and a search that has to be summoned is a search that gets used less. What gives it room is the four text links waiting for a wide screen — from 1280 up the bar carries logo, Shop, all four links, the box, the icons and both buttons; between 768 and 1280 the links stand down and the box stays, because logo, Shop, search and account is the set a buyer actually works with; below 768 the box becomes the icon again, since on a phone it would leave room for nothing else. The links are never lost, only relocated: they are in the Shop menu, the burger and the footer.

Item: Filter by business or practice
Why it matters: The client supplied the eighteen trades they sell to, with codes, and asked for them as a filter. A dental clinic and a cafe buy from almost disjoint halves of a 2,057-product catalogue, and neither wants to start at Medical Consumables and work it out.
Notes: Built 19 Aug 2026. A Business / practice section under Category, shut by default because it is a shortcut rather than a step, and open when a trade is chosen so the filter in force is visible. Choosing one narrows the products AND the category list — a dental clinic sees Dental, PPE and Cleaning rather than eleven departments reading zero — and clicking the chosen one again clears it, so escaping does not depend on finding Clear all. The client's codes travel in the URL (?business=BT-DEN) rather than the labels, so wording can change without breaking a shared link. General Business and Hospital & Day Surgery narrow NOTHING by design: one is the fallback so nobody is blocked, the other buys across the whole catalogue. An unrecognised code narrows nothing either, rather than emptying the page.

Item: What each trade buys is our guess, not the client's
Why it matters: The eighteen business types are the client's. The departments each one shops in were mapped by reasoning about the trade, because nothing in the catalogue says which business a product suits — there is no attribute, and 1,997 of the 2,057 products are invented samples anyway.
Notes: Raised 19 Aug 2026 with FE-44 so the guesswork is visible rather than buried in a component. Every mapping is in one table, pure and tested, in src/lib/business-types.ts — correcting it is editing a list, not hunting through screens, and the tests already assert that no mapping points at a department that does not exist. Worth a read by somebody who sells to these trades: a vet gets Pet Care plus the clinical departments, a cafe gets Kitchen, Cleaning and PPE and is deliberately kept out of the clinical half, a gym gets cleaning, first aid and PPE. Also to confirm: Office & Facility arrived without a code and is currently BT-OFF, following the pattern of the seventeen the client did give. This becomes far more than a filter question when the real catalogue lands (DA-01), since the same table is what a signup flow would use to decide what a new account sees first.

Item: A product performance report, and what to make our own
Why it matters: The client asked what earns the most on margin and sales, what is bought most, and anything similar that would help decide what to put an AussieMed label on. Nothing reported on products at all: the existing reports cover customers and suppliers.
Notes: Built 19 Aug 2026 at /admin/products/reports, behind a Products|Reports tab pair like the customer and supplier sections. Four tables. EARNS THE MOST is ranked by gross profit and not by margin, because sixty per cent of one box a year is worth less than twelve per cent of four hundred, and ranking by percentage is how a catalogue gets optimised for what nobody buys. MOVES THE MOST is units, and deliberately includes lines with no recorded cost, since volume is knowable without one. WORTH MAKING OUR OWN is a weighted score with its parts named on screen: volume 35, how many accounts buy it 25, HOW THIN THE MARGIN IS TODAY 25, and reorder frequency 15. That third part is the counter-intuitive one and the point of the whole report — the best own-brand candidate is the line where somebody else's brand takes most of the money, while the lines already earning well need no help. Every candidate carries its reasons in words, so the ranking can be argued with rather than believed. A line sold below cost scores well and is flagged as a PRICING problem first, because a print run is a slow way to fix what a price list fixes this afternoon. BY SHELF totals categories, because an own brand launches as a range. Rules are pure and tested 18 ways in src/lib/own-brand.ts; the data layer is admin-guarded in reports-data.ts and takes cost from the purchase allocations through margin.ts, so this report and the order screen cannot disagree. The screen LEADS WITH WHAT IT CANNOT SEE: orders, products sold, how many of them are costed, and units with no cost — on this database 88 of 126 units sold have no cost, and it says so rather than quietly ranking the nine it can measure. Below five orders it says plainly that a league table is noise.

Item: Borrow KAD3D's type and spacing, keep the AussieMed brand
Why it matters: Stated 23 Aug 2026. The client runs KAD3D (kad3d.com.au) as well and asked for the two sites to read as related. What was adopted is the confidence, not the identity: a larger heading scale and more air, plus Roboto in place of Figtree as the body stand-in. The navy, the red, the logo and Gilroy on headings are untouched, so DEC-02 stands rather than being reversed. The full monochrome restyle KAD3D uses was offered and declined.
Notes: Heading steps text-xl through text-5xl were raised in @theme; text-xs, sm and base were deliberately left alone because they carry the catalogue's dense rows and reflowing those costs more than the headings gain. The products listing title went from text-2xl to text-4xl — it had been smaller than the product names beneath it. Gilroy Bold and Light are real and self-hosted; only Regular and Medium were never delivered, which is still DA-08 and still why a stand-in is needed at all.

Item: Every country offers its own subdivisions, and its own word for them
Why it matters: Seventeen countries had a list and the other 135 had a free-text box, so most of the world typed its own province and we got Dubai, dubai and DXB again by a different door — the defect FE-39 was raised to close. All 152 now offer a list.
Notes: Requested 23 Aug 2026. The 17 curated lists in geo.ts are UNCHANGED — the UAE is still ordered Abu Dhabi and Dubai first, the US is still 50 states and DC rather than the package's 62 with territories, and matchSubdivision still compares against the same strings, so no stored address changes meaning. The other 135 are generated into src/data/subdivisions.json by npm run subdivisions:build, from country-region-data (MIT, devDependency). Labels were added for the generated countries too: Region for France, Prefecture for Japan, Canton for Switzerland. Anything unlisted falls back to State.

Item: Subdivisions are fetched one country at a time, not bundled
Why it matters: All 152 countries' lists come to about 3,300 entries. CountryFields renders on sign-up, checkout, a supplier and a customer, so bundling them would have put 37KB of places nobody selected into four client components — the weight problem BE-47 was raised about.
Notes: GET /api/v1/subdivisions/:country, cached a day in the browser and a week at the edge, since a country's provinces change on the timescale of constitutional reform. The 17 curated countries stay in the bundle, so an Emirati address — nearly all of them — costs no request and does not flicker. A failed or empty response falls back to the free-text box rather than an empty dropdown, because a form nobody can submit is worse than one that asks them to type.

Item: The phone field shows the flag of the country selected
Why it matters: The dialling prefix alone asks a person to know that +968 is Oman and +971 is not, and the two sit next to each other in the list. A flag is recognised without being read.
Notes: Requested 23 Aug 2026. Written first as a flag emoji, which needs no files at all, and thrown away: Windows ships no glyphs for regional indicator symbols, so Segoe UI Emoji renders the UAE flag as the letters AE. A trade buyer is overwhelmingly at an office desktop, so that version would have shown letters to most of the people it was meant to help. Now SVGs copied from flag-icons (MIT, devDependency) by npm run flags:build into public/flags — one is fetched at a time. A test asserts every country in COUNTRIES has a file on disk, so adding a country without rebuilding fails the suite rather than showing a broken image.

Item: Checkout offers on account or card, and prices both
Why it matters: Checkout offered one payment method and described card as ''a later decision''. A buyer deciding whether to open an account could not see what the alternative would cost them.
Notes: Requested 23 Aug 2026. On account is selectable and states the due date THIS account's terms produce, not a flat two weeks — asserting two weeks at an account agreed on Net30 would be telling them their invoice is due a fortnight early. Card is shown, priced against the order in front of the buyer, and disabled until Stripe is connected (IN-04). Wording lives in payment-options.ts because Prepaid is a different sentence, not a different word: concatenation produced ''Due 23 August 2026 — payable before dispatch from today'', which reached the rendered page before it was caught.

Item: Confirm the card fee that will be charged to customers
Why it matters: 2.9% + AED 1.00 is Stripe's published UAE rate as of Aug 2026, not a rate AussieMed has agreed. It is shown to buyers at checkout as what they will pay. A negotiated rate, an international-card loading or a currency-conversion charge all move it, and a figure quoted at checkout that differs from what is charged is a disputed card statement.
Notes: The constant is CARD_FEE_BASIS_POINTS / CARD_FEE_FIXED_FILS in src/lib/payment-options.ts, and cardFeeDescription() builds the wording from it, so correcting the rate is one edit and the copy follows. Must be confirmed before Stripe goes live — the figure is on screen now.

Item: Confirm that passing the card fee to the customer is permitted
Why it matters: The client's instruction is that the card charge is paid by the buyer, not absorbed. Surcharging a card payment is restricted by Visa and Mastercard scheme rules in many markets and is regulated in the UAE. If it is not permitted, the fee has to be absorbed or built into pricing, which changes margins rather than just wording.
Notes: Raised 23 Aug 2026 when the card option was built. Needs a merchant agreement and, if in doubt, the acquirer's answer in writing — not a developer's reading of the rules. The mechanism works either way: cardFeeFils() returns the surcharge and totalWithCardFeeFils() adds it, so absorbing it instead means not calling the second one. Nothing is charged today, so this blocks Stripe going live rather than blocking the build.

Item: Confirm Net14 as the default terms for a new trade account
Why it matters: Stated 23 Aug 2026: an account order should be ''finalised in 2 weeks''. Net14 did not exist — terms were Prepaid, Net7, Net30, Net60 — and AC-09 had recorded that trade buyers usually expect 30 days. Fourteen days is tighter than the norm this register assumed, so it is worth confirming rather than inferring.
Notes: Net14 is added and is the default for a new account. Existing accounts keep the terms they were agreed — the default moved, nothing already promised did. Credit limits (AC-09) are still not modelled.

Item: A customer can download their order as a PDF
Why it matters: An order could be read on screen and nowhere else. A trade buyer needs a copy to send to their accounts department, attach to a purchase order, or open again in a month, and had nothing to send.
Notes: Requested 23 Aug 2026. HTML plus the browser's print dialogue, the same choice PrintableDoc already records for the three admin documents: a PDF library is a dependency whose output nobody can check without running it, and Save as PDF is in every print dialogue. DELIBERATELY NOT CALLED A TAX INVOICE — AC-04 is open because these documents are not FTA-compliant, and a customer-downloadable page showing a VAT breakdown is the easiest thing here to file as an invoice; it says what it is, says the invoice follows, and runs the same invoiceCompliance check the admin document runs. Access repeats the order page's rule (admin, owner, or a guest holding the cart that placed it) rather than trusting the page that links to it, since the route is reachable on its own; verified from a clean browser that a stranger gets 404 for a real reference and a missing one alike. PrintableDoc gained the print-document class so a document rendered inside the shop layout does not print wrapped in the site header and footer.

Item: The order PDF needs a browser on the server
Why it matters: Clicking Download PDF renders the HTML order confirmation with headless Chromium via Playwright, so the file and the screen cannot disagree. That puts a browser in the runtime path: Playwright is now a runtime dependency, not a dev one, and it needs its Chromium binary present. A plain serverless function has neither, and a 300MB dependency does not fit in one.
Notes: Raised 23 Aug 2026, when the customer PDF was built. Decide alongside IN-01 (hosting) rather than at deploy. Works on any host that runs a long-lived Node process with the browser installed. On a serverless host the options are a Chromium build made for it (@sparticuz/chromium and puppeteer-core), a separate render service, or dropping to a PDF library and writing the document a second time in its primitives — which is what rendering the real page was chosen to avoid. Nothing is broken today: the site is not deployed, and /orders/REF/document still prints without any of this.

Item: The order track is coloured by stage
Why it matters: The track read in the five status tones: green behind, blue where it is now, grey ahead. The client wants it to read as a thing ripening instead — red on arrival, orange while it is prepared, light green once it is moving, solid green when it lands.
Notes: Requested 23 Aug 2026. The ramp is its own CSS variables, NOT a remapping of the five tones: in the tone system red means stopped, and tone-colours.ts is deliberate that the mapping is meaning rather than preference. A new order is not stopped, it is at the beginning, and folding the two together would have made red mean both. The track is the only place the ramp is used, and a cancelled order leaves the track rather than colouring it, so red-at-the-start and red-for-cancelled never share a control. The whole reached portion takes the CURRENT stage colour, because solid green as delivered is the test and a fixed per-segment ramp would have left a delivered order starting in red for ever. Colour still is not the only carrier: the current step is the only one in bold, it is the only one with a glyph, and the stage is written in words.

Item: Unpaid is red, the way paid is green
Why it matters: Unpaid was grey, on the reading that an invoice with thirty days to run is nothing to worry about. The client reads the axis as the money one — it is either in or it is not — and wants a customer to see that at a glance.
Notes: Requested 23 Aug 2026. Unpaid moved from the resting tone to stopped. IT ALSO BROKE SOMETHING THAT ONLY A TEST CAUGHT: needsAttention() derived the admin action queue from the tone, so turning the pill red put every open invoice in the business into the queue at once. The queue answers whether somebody must do something, which is not the same question as what colour the pill is, and it is now decoupled — plain not-yet-due Unpaid is excluded, while DueSoon and Overdue still come through. Two tests pin that so it cannot silently regress.

Item: Decide whether the rest of the payment colours should follow Unpaid
Why it matters: With Unpaid red, the payment axis was no longer ordered by urgency: plain Unpaid was red while Due soon was amber, so the more pressing of the two looked calmer. Unpaid also shared red with Overdue and the two were told apart only by their words.
Notes: Answered 24 Aug 2026, one day after it was raised. The axis reads as a temperature rather than a binary: orange while the money is owed, red once it is late, green when it is in, blue when it went back. Unpaid and Overdue no longer share a colour, which was the substance of the concern — the state that needs chasing is now the only red one. A test asserts those two stay different.

Item: Invoices moved from Spending to Orders, and the list gained filters
Why it matters: The invoice table sat on Spending, which answers what did we spend — a question about totals. A list of individual references each linking to its own invoice is a question about orders, so somebody chasing one invoice opened the reports screen to find it. Orders itself had one filter, branch.
Notes: Requested 23 Aug 2026, taking the filter set from the client's operations tool per DEC-20: search on reference or their own PO, plus status, payment, branch and period, all in the URL so a link to exactly what is on screen can be sent on. The table gained Status and Payment columns and a footer that totals only the rows shown — a sum ignoring the filter above it is a number somebody quotes at their accountant. Spending keeps a pointer rather than losing the section silently. AdminFilters was renamed UrlFilters: nothing about it was ever admin-only, and a component named for the first screen that used it is one nobody reuses.

Item: Order filtering is derived, not queried
Why it matters: Payment status is not a stored word that can be compared in a query. Overdue and Due soon are the stored status with the passage of time folded in, so a filter matching on the column would return nothing for Overdue while rows on the same screen showed Overdue pills.
Notes: src/lib/order-filters.ts is pure and takes the clock, with 13 tests — including the one that matters: an invoice whose column still reads Unpaid but whose due date has passed must be found by the Overdue filter and NOT by the Unpaid one. Branch stays in the query since it is a real column. The rest runs in memory over the 100-order cap, which is one honest pass rather than a second definition of what overdue means. If the cap is ever lifted this is the thing to revisit.

Item: Payment pills read as a temperature, and lose their glyphs
Why it matters: Paid carried a tick and Unpaid a cross, which said in a symbol what the word beside it already said. The colours also did not line up with how the client thinks about money owed.
Notes: Set by the client 24 Aug 2026: Unpaid orange, Overdue red, Paid green, Refunded blue — Refunded was grey, which filed money moving the other way under nothing is happening. StatusMeaning gained an optional glyph override so a single status can drop its tone's symbol; nothing outside the payment axis is touched, and Overdue KEEPS its cross deliberately, being the one payment state somebody must act on and the one that has to survive a mono printer. StatusDot falls back to a filled circle where a glyph is dropped, since a dot has no label beside it to carry the meaning. Closes AC-18.

Item: Couriers are a managed list, not free text
Why it matters: Two screens asked for a courier and both were free-text boxes — an admin dispatching an order to a customer, and a supplier in the portal saying what is on its way to us. Free text is how Aramex, aramex and ARAMEX become three couriers, found out by whoever first tries to compare carriers on late deliveries.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026. New Courier table plus migration 20260823155353_couriers, added to the admin Settings screen with add and remove. THE ORDER STILL STORES THE NAME AS TEXT and there is no foreign key: an order records what was true when it shipped, so removing a courier must not rewrite what last year's delivery notes say. Removal is therefore an archive, which the screen says out loud, and each row shows how many orders name it so that taking one off the list is an informed decision. Duplicates are refused case-insensitively, which a SQLite unique index would not have caught. Reading the list is unguarded because a supplier needs it and public carrier names are not a secret; every write requires an admin and is audited.

Item: The courier pickers fall back to a text box when the list is empty
Why it matters: A dropdown with nothing in it is a form nobody can complete, and the courier list starts empty on a fresh database. Without a fallback this change would have broken dispatch on both screens on the day it shipped.
Notes: CourierPicker renders a select when there are couriers and the original free-text input when there are none, so both screens keep working until the first courier is added. Whatever is already stored is always an option even when it is not on the list — an archived courier, or a name typed before the list existed — so opening an old order and saving it cannot silently blank a courier that has been delivering parcels for a year. Same rule the address subdivision picker follows.

Item: A supplier is no longer told whether they are primary or backup
Why it matters: The portal showed each supplier their rank on every item, on the reasoning that it explained a quiet month. It is AussieMed's commercial position, not theirs: a backup who knows they are the backup prices and prioritises differently, and one who is demoted learns it from a screen rather than from us.
Notes: Client's decision, 24 Aug 2026, reversing the earlier reasoning. listMySupplies no longer SELECTS rank rather than selecting and dropping it — this file's standing rule, so a column that is never read cannot be leaked by the next person who adds a field to the returned object. The pill is off SupplyRow. Verified there is no remaining mention of rank anywhere under the supplier-facing path apart from the comment explaining its absence.

Item: Cover can be set from the admin, one pack or many
Why it matters: Primary and backup existed on ProductSupply from the start and nothing in the admin could set them. Cover arrived with a catalogue import and changing it meant importing again — a poor way to move one line to a different supplier and no way at all to move forty.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026. New screen at /admin/suppliers/cover with per-row selects and a bulk bar, filtered by item, SKU, their part number, supplier, category, and a gaps filter for packs missing a primary or a backup. TWO CONSTRAINTS SHAPE THE WRITE and are why the obvious implementation is wrong: unique(skuId, rank) and unique(skuId, supplierId) mean setting a primary is four different operations depending on where that supplier already stands. Promoting the existing backup is a SWAP, which needs three statements and a parked rank inside a transaction, because SQLite checks the unique index per statement rather than at commit. Ranks move, not supplier ids, so each supplier's cost and part number travel with them — verified through the UI: costs 12154 and 14211 followed their own suppliers across a promotion. A reassignment to a NEW supplier clears cost and part number deliberately, since what one supplier charges is not what another charges and carrying it over would put a wrong figure on a margin report. Bulk reports what it skipped and why rather than a bare count.

Item: Supply rank is nullable, so a supplier can offer an item without holding cover
Why it matters: ProductSupply allowed exactly two suppliers per pack — unique(skuId, rank) with rank Primary or Backup — so a supplier adding an item to their own list had nowhere to go. Every slot might be taken, and letting them claim one would let a supplier make themselves our primary, which is the opposite of what the Cover screen exists for.
Notes: Migration 20260823162752_supply_offers. rank is now nullable and NULL means an offer — this supplier can supply this pack — rather than cover. SQLite treats NULLs as DISTINCT in a unique index, so any number of suppliers can offer a pack while exactly one Primary and one Backup remain enforced; both halves verified against the real database. isApproved was added alongside, false only where a supplier self-added while approvals are on. No new table, and every existing row kept its rank through the rebuild.

Item: An offer could have been treated as the primary supplier by the buying run
Why it matters: purchasing.ts mapped rank with `supply.rank === ''Backup'' ? ''Backup'' : ''Primary''`, so anything that was not the literal string Backup became Primary — and null is not the string Backup. The moment supply rank became nullable, a supplier who merely offered an item would have been handed our purchase orders for it.
Notes: Found while making rank nullable on 24 Aug 2026, before any null existed, so nothing was ever mis-ordered. Both readers now exclude offers in the QUERY rather than in the mapping: purchasing.ts for the buying run, and margin-data.ts, which would additionally have put a supplier with no agreed cost onto a margin report. The lesson is the defaulting ternary: `x === a ? a : b` silently claims every other value is b, and it is only safe while the set really has two members. TypeScript caught the second reader; nothing would have caught the first.

Item: Purchase orders carry a payment status the supplier can see
Why it matters: A purchase order tracked only where the goods were. Whether we had paid the supplier was not recorded anywhere, so a supplier wanting to know had to ring and ask, and nobody here could answer from a screen.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026. Migration 20260823173331_purchase_order_payment adds paymentStatus, paidFils, paidAt and paymentDueOn to PurchaseOrder, mirroring what a customer order already carries. Overdue and Due soon are NOT stored: paymentStatusOf derives them from the due date, so an invoice that fell due yesterday reads Overdue today with no nightly job to forget — verified end to end, where a stored PartiallyPaid with a past due date showed the supplier Overdue. Set from the admin purchase order screen, which says on the panel that the supplier sees it, since that is the one thing on that screen which is not staff-only. paidAt is stamped when the status first becomes Paid and cleared if it moves back off, because a date that survives being un-paid is one somebody later quotes as when the money went out. An amount above the order value is refused rather than clamped: quietly reducing a typo hides it from whoever reconciles the bank statement.

Item: The admin orders payment filter found no overdue invoices
Why it matters: Overdue and Due soon are never stored — they are the stored word plus the passage of time, derived by paymentStatusOf so a screen is right when it is looked at. The admin list filtered on the column instead, so Overdue matched ZERO rows while ten invoices sat overdue in front of it, and Unpaid silently included every one of them. On a screen used to chase money that is the wrong answer in the reassuring direction, which is the direction nobody double-checks.
Notes: Found 24 Aug 2026 while confirming a separate report about the Paid filter, which turned out to work correctly. Fixed by deriving in the QUERY rather than in memory: the list pages and sorts in the database, so filtering afterwards would return short pages and wrong counts. paymentFilterWhere expresses the same rules as a where clause and lives beside paymentStatusOf; a test drives all 35 combinations of stored status and due date through BOTH and asserts they agree, so changing one without the other now fails. Overdue went from 0 to 10 and Unpaid from 20 to 14. The clause is nested under AND rather than spread in, because the search box already puts an OR on that object and a second OR key would have replaced it — searching and filtering at once would have dropped the search silently; verified that combination separately.

Item: A supplier's whole purchase order card opens the order
Why it matters: Only the reference number was clickable, which is a small target on a card-sized row that is entirely about one order.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026. A stretched link rather than wrapping the card in an anchor: the card contains the Acknowledge button, and a button inside a link is invalid HTML that browsers resolve by breaking one of the two. The reference stays the only real link and its ::after covers the card; the button is lifted above that overlay and still works, which was verified by clicking dead space at the bottom-right of a card and confirming it opened the order. One accepted consequence: text in the card is no longer selectable by dragging.

Item: A supplier can say how many of each line they can actually send
Why it matters: A supplier could acknowledge a whole order or say nothing. ''I can do eight of the ten'' happened on the phone and never reached the screen the buying run reads, so a short delivery was first discovered when it arrived.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026. Migration 20260823221553_supplier_confirmed_quantities adds qtyConfirmed to PurchaseOrderLine. THREE QUANTITIES, THREE FACTS: qtyOrdered is what we asked, qtyConfirmed what they promised, qtyReceived what turned up — a short delivery against a full promise is a supplier problem, one against a short promise is something we were told and did not act on. NULL means not said yet and is kept distinct from a confirmed zero, so nothing is defaulted on their behalf. A counter appears only where there is something to count: a one-unit line gets a yes/no, since a spinner offering 0 or 1 is a worse checkbox. ''I can supply all of it'' fills the boxes rather than submitting, so the person sees what they are about to promise. Over-ordering is refused server-side naming the item and the quantity, verified by stripping the client-side max and posting anyway — nothing was written.

Item: A supplier sees their back orders, grouped by order
Why it matters: A supplier could tell us they were short and then had nowhere to see what they were still on the hook for. The shortfall existed as a number and appeared on no screen.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026. Always on the purchase orders screen, empty or not — a panel that appears only when something is wrong is one nobody learns the location of, and ''nothing outstanding'' is worth saying to somebody who has just answered a difficult order. Grouped by purchase order and sorted newest first, because a supplier works order by order rather than item by item. Each line says what they can send of what was asked and carries a plain ''N missing'' label. The wording is deliberately not accusatory: a supplier who tells us they are short is doing the thing we want.

Item: Back orders can be re-sourced to another supplier, and the demand moves with them
Why it matters: When a supplier could not supply, covering it elsewhere meant raising an order by hand and remembering to unpick the original allocations. Forgetting that leaves customer demand attached to a line that will never deliver.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026. /admin/purchasing/backorders lists every confirmed shortfall grouped by order; ticking lines and choosing a supplier raises ONE draft purchase order for the total, which is the order a buyer would actually place. THE ALLOCATIONS ARE THE WHOLE DIFFICULTY: a PurchaseAllocation ties a purchase order line to the customer order item it was bought for, and outstandingDemand counts an allocated unit as covered — so leaving them on a line that will not deliver means the daily run never re-buys them and the customer waits for something nobody is sending. Re-sourcing MOVES them, largest allocation first so the fewest rows are split. Verified end to end: a line ordered 2 and confirmed 1 moved exactly 1 unit to the new order, left 1 behind, and total demand across the affected order items was 2 before and 2 after. The original line is never rewritten — it is a document we sent and it records what was asked and what was promised. Cost and part number come from the NEW supplier, never carried over, since a cost is an agreement with a particular company. The arithmetic is pure in backorder-maths.ts with 14 tests, including that a null qtyConfirmed is silence rather than a refusal and must not be re-sourced.

Item: A supplier can browse the catalogue and add what they stock
Why it matters: AussieMed decided every item a supplier covered, and the portal said so — get in touch and we will add them. That is a phone call for something the supplier knows better than we do.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026. /business-portal/supplies/add lists active catalogue items the supplier does not already have, searchable and filterable by category, with our SKU in its own column since their code and ours rarely match. Items already on their list are excluded rather than greyed out: a list of things you cannot pick is one you read twice. Each row has its own form and its own action state so a refusal lands against the row that caused it, not at the top of a hundred. ADDING IS AN OFFER, NOT COVER — the row is created with a null rank, which the buying run excludes in its query, so nothing a supplier does here puts them in line for a purchase order. The page says that plainly rather than leaving them to wonder why nothing arrived. Verified end to end: added item stored rank null, appeared on their own supply list, and appeared on the admin's unallocated screen as an offer.

Item: Admin can see products with no supplier at all
Why it matters: Nothing listed items nobody was allocated to supply. The buying run reaches one and has nowhere to go, and the first anybody hears of it is a customer order that cannot be sourced.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026. /admin/products/unallocated, as a No supplier tab beside Products and Reports. NOT the same question as Cover's no-primary filter, which finds items whose primary slot is empty but where somebody may still hold the backup; this finds items with no cover at either rank. Offers are shown beside each row, because the answer is often already on the screen — a supplier who added the item to their own list has told us they can supply it. Allocate links through to the Cover screen filtered to that SKU rather than repeating rank selects here: the same decision in two places is two places free to disagree.

Item: A switch decides whether suppliers' own additions wait for approval
Why it matters: Letting suppliers add items immediately is the client's preference, but they asked to be able to turn that off without a deploy.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026, built with the self-add. Setting supplyOffersNeedApproval, off by default, toggled from admin Settings; on, additions arrive with isApproved false. Either way the addition is only an offer and never grants cover, which the setting's own wording says because the word approval invites the opposite assumption. A supplier can remove an offer of their own but NOT a row where they hold primary or backup — letting them drop agreed cover from their side would take a line out of the buying run with nothing said to anybody here.

Item: A supplier can see, read and download their monthly invoice
Why it matters: Suppliers had no view of what they were owed. Both sides worked from separate spreadsheets, and the first anybody knew of a disagreement was a payment somebody disputed.
Notes: Requested 24 Aug 2026. /business-portal/invoices lists a month per row with total and payment status, newest first; the month opens as a document through PrintableDoc, which gained an optional backLabel and downloadHref. SELF-BILLED — the supplier does not raise one and we do not key one in, and the page says so, because a supplier expecting to invoice us needs telling once that they do not have to.
